candidates.rationale: For building an enduring pop-culture persona while using that platform for charitable work, LGBTQ+ advocacy, and a notably candid public life.
For turning a solitary school strike into a global youth climate movement centered on climate science and public accountability.
For building World Central Kitchen around the practical idea that people in disasters and conflicts need good food quickly, delivered through local kitchens and cooks.
For organizing Christian and Muslim women in a nonviolent peace movement that helped pressure Liberia toward an end to civil war.
For teaching science in an under-resourced Kenyan school, supporting students materially, and helping rural students reach national and international science competitions.
For Indigenous-led work protecting Waorani territory, Amazon rainforest, and community self-determination in Ecuador.
For building and sustaining educational access for Afghan girls, including co-founding the School of Leadership, Afghanistan.
For decades of work against child labor and trafficking through rescue, rehabilitation, education, organizing, and international advocacy.
For repeatedly iterating real engineering systems aimed at removing plastic from oceans and rivers rather than leaving the idea at the prototype stage.
For leaving a conventional culinary career to build recurring food and care services for homeless and mentally ill people in Madurai.
For turning the murder of his son into long-term youth-violence prevention and restorative-justice work, including collaboration with the family of the person who killed him.
For helping build long-running educational, residential, health, and women's services in Surkhet, Nepal through BlinkNow.
For pairing an extraordinary cultural career with sustained philanthropy, especially childhood literacy through the Imagination Library and major support for communities in need.
For making wildlife conservation and public education unusually accessible to a mass audience while supporting habitat and species protection.
For treating children as people worthy of emotional honesty, patience, and dignity, and building decades of public television around that premise.
For leading nonviolent campaigns against racial segregation and disenfranchisement and helping make civil-rights reform a national political imperative.
For judging a 1983 Soviet missile-warning alert as a likely false alarm instead of escalating it through the chain of command, reducing the risk of catastrophic retaliation.
For linking tree planting, women's livelihoods, environmental protection, and democratic participation through the Green Belt Movement.
For building a large, privately supported network of ambulances, shelters, orphanages, rehabilitation services, and other social care across Pakistan.
For providing medicine, refuge, and institution-building through decades of conflict in Somalia.
For founding BRAC and building large-scale systems for education, health, livelihoods, agriculture, and poverty reduction.
For issuing transit visas that helped thousands of Jewish refugees escape Europe during World War II despite substantial professional and personal risk.
For participating in a rescue network that smuggled Jewish children from the Warsaw Ghetto, arranged identities and shelter, and protected information about them under arrest and torture.
For pioneering child-centered ideas about dignity and rights, running institutions around those principles, and refusing to abandon the children in his care during the Holocaust.
For agricultural research and crop-breeding programs that substantially increased food production while also leaving a consequential debate about the costs of Green Revolution agriculture.
For building health systems around the principle that poor communities deserve excellent medical care and for making structural inequality a practical health-system problem.
For transforming the study of chimpanzees through long-term field research and using that scientific prominence for decades of conservation and public education.
For his central role in opposing apartheid, negotiating South Africa's democratic transition, and promoting reconciliation while serving as president.
For escaping slavery, repeatedly returning to guide others to freedom through the Underground Railroad, serving the Union cause, and later advocating for women's suffrage.

Survived a 2012 assassination attempt for advocating girls' education in Swat, then turned the attention into the Malala Fund, which backs girls'-education programs and advocacy across a dozen countries. A direct case for education as a life-or-death issue, not an abstraction.
candidates.objections: Some critics argue Western media flattened her into a symbol detached from Pakistani domestic politics and the Taliban's broader record in the region; the profile should keep her own advocacy work, not just the attack, at the center.

candidates.rationale: Gynecological surgeon who founded Panzi Hospital in Bukavu, treating tens of thousands of survivors of wartime sexual violence while campaigning internationally against its use as a weapon of war. Shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: His outspoken criticism of Congolese and regional governments over conflict minerals and militia violence is politically contested; keep the profile centered on the documented medical and advocacy work rather than adjudicating regional politics.

candidates.rationale: Artist and activist whose work (Sunflower Seeds, the Sichuan earthquake student-name project, refugee-crisis installations) repeatedly turns state secrecy and mass harm into something the public cannot look away from.
candidates.objections: Detained and beaten by Chinese authorities in 2011; some critics separately argue his large-scale international art-market success sits uneasily with his activist framing. Both threads belong in a full profile.

candidates.rationale: Former Mozambican education minister who became a leading international voice on children affected by armed conflict, authoring the landmark 1996 UN report on the subject, and co-founded The Elders with Nelson Mandela.
candidates.objections: Her decades of work predate and extend well beyond her marriages to Samora Machel and Nelson Mandela; the profile should avoid reducing her record to a footnote of either man's biography.

candidates.rationale: K'iche' Maya activist who documented the Guatemalan military's violence against Indigenous communities during the civil war and became an international voice for Indigenous rights, winning the 1992 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: A 1999 investigation found some details in her acclaimed memoir 'I, Rigoberta Menchú' were altered or composited; this is a real, documented controversy that belongs in the profile alongside the substantiated core of her family's persecution and her later advocacy.

candidates.rationale: Former Jain monk who walked roughly 8,000 miles for nuclear disarmament in the 1960s, then co-founded Schumacher College, an influential center for ecological and holistic education in England.
candidates.objections: No major documented controversy found; keep the profile focused on his verifiable institutional work (the peace walk, Resurgence magazine, Schumacher College) rather than uncritically adopting his own spiritual framing as fact.

candidates.rationale: Afghan rapper who, facing her own forced marriage, wrote and performed 'Brides for Sale', turning a private crisis into a public campaign against child marriage that also became the subject of the documentary 'Sonita'.
candidates.objections: The documentary's own director paid for Sonita's schooling and intervened directly in her family's decision, which raised its own debate about filmmaker involvement in a subject's life; that tension is worth including rather than presenting the story as a clean rescue narrative.

candidates.rationale: Hiroshima bombing survivor who spent decades giving firsthand testimony and organizing internationally, and delivered the acceptance speech when ICAN won the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize for the campaign to abolish nuclear weapons.
candidates.objections: Born in 1932; living status specifically needs re-verification at ingest time rather than assumed from this docket, per the gallery's standard living/deceased recheck.

candidates.rationale: Founded Ethiopia Reads after working as a librarian in the United States, building children's libraries, a donkey-mobile-library program, and children's book publishing in a country with very limited access to books in local languages.
candidates.objections: Publicly available sourcing on scale and current program status is thinner than for larger NGOs; the profile should be careful to cite specific, dated program facts rather than repeating promotional figures unverified.

candidates.rationale: Lenca activist who co-founded COPINH and led opposition to the Agua Zarca dam on land sacred to the Lenca people, winning the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2015 before being assassinated in her home in 2016.
candidates.objections: Her killing led to convictions including a dam-company executive; the case remains a documented example of violence against Indigenous and environmental defenders in Honduras and should be presented with that documented outcome, not left as an open mystery.

candidates.rationale: Escaped bonded labor in a carpet factory at age 10, then became an internationally known campaigner against child labor and bonded servitude before being killed in 1995 at age 12.
candidates.objections: The circumstances and motive of his killing remain disputed between accounts blaming the 'carpet mafia' and accounts describing an unrelated local dispute; both versions should be represented rather than presenting either as settled fact.

candidates.rationale: Writer and television producer who led the Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People, campaigning against oil-industry pollution in the Niger Delta, before being executed by Nigeria's military government in 1995.
candidates.objections: His trial was widely condemned internationally as a sham; Shell's role and later settlement of a related civil suit (without admitting liability) is a documented, contested part of the story that belongs in the profile.

candidates.rationale: Soviet naval officer serving on a submarine during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis whose refusal to authorize a nuclear torpedo launch, when the other two required officers voted to fire, is widely credited with helping avert nuclear war.
candidates.objections: Details of the incident were classified for decades and rely on accounts that emerged well after the fact; the profile should attribute specifics to the historians/participants who documented them rather than presenting a single cinematic account as certain.

candidates.rationale: Rubber tapper who organized fellow seringueiros to defend the Amazon rainforest from clear-cutting through nonviolent human blockades ('empates') and helped establish the extractive-reserve model, before being assassinated by ranchers in 1988.
candidates.objections: His killers (a rancher and his son) were convicted, escaped, and were later recaptured; that documented resolution should be included rather than leaving the case open-ended.

candidates.rationale: Physicist and chemist who discovered polonium and radium, developed mobile X-ray units used on WWI battlefields, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
candidates.objections: She died of aplastic anemia almost certainly caused by her own prolonged radiation exposure, a documented cost of pioneering work done before radiation's dangers were understood; worth including rather than treating her death as unrelated to the science.

candidates.rationale: Businessman who witnessed the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in 1859 and, appalled by the lack of care for wounded soldiers, led the effort that created the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions, sharing the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
candidates.objections: He died in poverty and relative obscurity after a business scandal derailed his earlier career; the profile should include that fall alongside the humanitarian legacy rather than presenting a purely triumphant arc.

candidates.rationale: One of the Dutch citizens who helped hide Anne Frank's family and others in an Amsterdam annex for two years, and who preserved Anne Frank's diary after the family's arrest, later helping bring it to publication.
candidates.objections: Gies herself repeatedly insisted she was not a hero and that others did far more with far less recognition; the profile should reflect her own stated framing rather than a purely mythologized 'lone rescuer' narrative.

candidates.rationale: Novaya Gazeta journalist whose reporting on human-rights abuses during the Chechen wars and on Russian government and military conduct made her one of the most prominent critical voices in Russian journalism, before she was assassinated in her apartment building in 2006.
candidates.objections: Several men were later convicted as the killers, but who ordered the killing remains officially unresolved; the profile should say precisely what has and has not been legally established.

candidates.rationale: Lawyer who gave up a comfortable career to found Anandwan, a self-sustaining community built by and for people affected by leprosy and disability at a time when leprosy carried severe social stigma in India.
candidates.objections: Later in life he also campaigned against the Narmada dam projects, a still-contested development debate; that advocacy should be described factually rather than as settled consensus.

candidates.rationale: Journalist and activist who founded Women Journalists Without Chains and became a leading voice of Yemen's 2011 uprising. In 2011 she became the first Arab woman and among the youngest people to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Her ties to Yemen's Islah party and later criticism of Gulf states have drawn political objections; the profile should center her documented nonviolent organizing.

candidates.rationale: Yazidi survivor of captivity by ISIS who turned her testimony into a campaign for accountability and for survivors of sexual violence. Shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Some Yazidi and Iraqi commentators dispute how advocacy funds and attention are directed; no serious dispute of her core testimony has been found.

candidates.rationale: Leads the Elman Peace and Human Rights Centre in Mogadishu, which runs rehabilitation for former child soldiers and support for survivors of sexual violence, continuing work begun by her parents.
candidates.objections: Some critics question the role of international donors in Somali civil society; no personal controversy found beyond that.

candidates.rationale: Co-founded Prajwala in Hyderabad, which has rescued and reintegrated thousands of women and children from sex trafficking, and campaigns for policy change and public awareness.
candidates.objections: Her publicity methods and views on prostitution law have been debated by other rights groups; the profile should present her rehabilitation record and note that debate.

candidates.rationale: Iranian lawyer who has defended political prisoners, women protesting compulsory hijab, and juvenile offenders, and has herself been repeatedly imprisoned. Received the 2012 Sakharov Prize.
candidates.objections: Her legal status and health under detention have changed repeatedly; verify current circumstances at ingest time.

candidates.rationale: Founder of the Viasna Human Rights Centre, which documents political imprisonment in Belarus. Jailed since 2021 and shared the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Belarusian authorities convicted him on tax-evasion and smuggling charges widely regarded by rights groups as politically motivated; confirm his current status at ingest time.

candidates.rationale: Physician who ran clinics and schools for Afghan women and refugees, then chaired the Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission. Kept documenting abuses across successive governments.
candidates.objections: Her work drew threats and criticism from conservative factions; no personal misconduct found.

candidates.rationale: Economist who founded Uyghur Online to promote dialogue, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2014 on separatism charges. Received the 2019 Sakharov Prize.
candidates.objections: Chinese authorities call him a separatist; rights organizations and most governments call the charges unfounded. Keep the profile to his documented scholarship and writing.

candidates.rationale: Founded the Rise Up Movement to amplify African climate voices; drew wide attention after being cropped out of a 2020 press photo, and continues to campaign on climate finance and loss and damage.
candidates.objections: Some argue youth climate advocacy has limited policy effect; no personal controversy found.

candidates.rationale: Heads the Center for Civil Liberties in Kyiv, which has documented war crimes since 2014 and pushed for international accountability. Shared the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Some critics have questioned her positions on negotiations and accountability; the profile should stay on her documentation work.

candidates.rationale: Archbishop of San Salvador who publicly denounced military killings and repression, and was assassinated while celebrating Mass in 1980. Canonized in 2018.
candidates.objections: Some Salvadorans and church figures criticized his politics as too aligned with the left; supporters note he condemned violence from all sides.

candidates.rationale: Anglican archbishop and Nobel laureate who led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid and argued that forgiveness and accountability belong together.
candidates.objections: Critics on multiple sides faulted the TRC's limits, and his statements on Israel and other issues drew objections; note both.

candidates.rationale: Swedish diplomat who issued protective passports and sheltered tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest in 1944, then vanished in Soviet custody in 1945.
candidates.objections: His fate remains unresolved and the exact number saved is estimated, not exact; flag that uncertainty.

candidates.rationale: Portuguese consul in Bordeaux who defied his government's orders and issued visas to thousands of refugees fleeing the Nazi invasion of France. He was punished and died in poverty.
candidates.objections: Exact visa counts vary by source; no personal controversy found.

candidates.rationale: Member of the White Rose group who distributed leaflets against the regime and was executed in 1943 at age 21.
candidates.objections: Later memory has sometimes simplified the group's motives; keep the profile close to primary sources.

candidates.rationale: Anti-apartheid activist who built the Black Consciousness movement and community health and education projects, and died in police custody in 1977.
candidates.objections: Historians debate parts of his movement's ideology and its relation to other anti-apartheid groups; keep to documented work.

candidates.rationale: Saudi journalist and columnist murdered inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 after writing critically of the Saudi government.
candidates.objections: His earlier closeness to Saudi establishment figures and Islamist movements is debated; present that alongside his later writing.

candidates.rationale: Zen teacher who organized relief and peace efforts during the Vietnam War, was exiled, and founded Plum Village. His writing on mindfulness reached a global readership.
candidates.objections: Some Vietnamese critics disputed his neutrality during the war; note this alongside his humanitarian work.

candidates.rationale: Literary critic and co-author of Charter 08, imprisoned for subversion; won the 2010 Nobel Peace Prize and died in custody in 2017.
candidates.objections: Chinese authorities call him a criminal, and some earlier comments of his about Western models and the Iraq War drew criticism.

candidates.rationale: Playwright and dissident imprisoned under communism who became the last president of Czechoslovakia and first of the Czech Republic.
candidates.objections: His presidency drew domestic criticism, including over amnesties and his support for the Iraq war; note these.

candidates.rationale: Co-founded Rappler and reported on disinformation and press freedom under the Duterte government; shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Faced Philippine tax-fraud and cyber-libel charges widely characterized internationally as politically motivated retaliation; state both the charges and that characterization as attributed claims, not settled fact.

candidates.rationale: Longtime editor of Novaya Gazeta, which lost six journalists (including Anna Politkovskaya) to killings tied to their reporting; shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize and auctioned his medal for Ukrainian refugee relief.
candidates.objections: Novaya Gazeta suspended Russian print/online operations in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine; his case sits directly inside an active geopolitical conflict, so framing needs care to describe facts without taking a side on the war itself.

candidates.rationale: Iran's first female judge before the 1979 revolution barred women from the bench; later a human rights lawyer representing dissidents, children, and women, and the first Iranian and first Muslim woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize (2003).
candidates.objections: Has lived in exile since 2009 and is outspokenly critical of the Iranian government, which disputes her legitimacy; politically charged subject, keep language factual/attributed.

candidates.rationale: Coordinated the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, which helped produce the 1997 Ottawa Treaty; shared the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found; verify current (2026) activity level and affiliations before publishing.

candidates.rationale: Trained nurse-midwife and former Somaliland foreign minister who built and funded the Edna Adan University Hospital in Hargeisa to reduce maternal and infant mortality and train midwives.
candidates.objections: Somaliland's disputed international statehood status complicates simple country/region metadata — note it as "Somaliland (unrecognized state within Somalia's internationally recognized borders)" rather than picking a side implicitly.

candidates.rationale: Co-founded what grew into the Women's Initiative The Gambia, organizing women to recycle plastic waste into saleable goods, address a visible pollution problem, and build local income.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found; public sourcing is thinner than for Nobel-tier figures — verify current program scale/status before treating any specific numbers as current.

candidates.rationale: First deafblind person to graduate from Harvard Law School; works as a disability rights lawyer and advocate for accessible technology.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found.

candidates.rationale: Catholic nun whose ministry to death-row inmates produced "Dead Man Walking" and decades of advocacy against capital punishment.
candidates.objections: Her work is advocacy on a genuinely contested policy question (capital punishment); present it as her position and record, not as a settled neutral conclusion.

candidates.rationale: Physicist known for low-cost UV water disinfection (UV Waterworks) and a fuel-efficient stove design (Berkeley-Darfur Stove) developed for displaced people in Darfur.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found; verify current institutional affiliation (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory / UC Berkeley) and retirement status.

candidates.rationale: Psychiatrist and researcher who pioneered task-shifting models that let trained lay counselors deliver mental health care in low-resource settings, expanding care access far beyond what specialist psychiatrists alone could reach.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found.

candidates.rationale: Palestinian physician whose three daughters were killed by Israeli tank fire during the 2009 Gaza war; wrote "I Shall Not Hate" and has since advocated for reconciliation and a peace-focused NGO connecting Israeli and Palestinian communities.
candidates.objections: His case sits directly inside the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Describe his own stated position (reconciling rather than hating) without the profile itself taking a side on the conflict's underlying political questions.

candidates.rationale: Samoan climate activist who has represented Pacific Island youth at UN climate conferences since her teens, centering small island states' existential stake in climate policy.
candidates.objections: Early-career; public record is thinner than older candidates in this pool — verify current activity and affiliations before publishing.

candidates.rationale: Guajajara leader and longtime Indigenous-rights organizer in Brazil, prominent in resisting Amazon deforestation and defending Indigenous land rights.
candidates.objections: Now serves as Brazil's Minister of Indigenous Peoples under the Lula government — an active partisan government role, not just activism. State the appointment as fact without the profile endorsing or opposing that administration.

candidates.rationale: Prominent young figure in Hong Kong's 2014 and 2019 pro-democracy protest movements, previously a leader of the now-disbanded Demosisto party.
candidates.objections: Highly contested politically between pro-democracy and Hong Kong/Chinese-government framings. She has stated publicly she will not return to Hong Kong, citing fear of arrest; attribute disputed claims to their source (her statements vs. government positions) rather than asserting either as fact.
candidates.region: Hong Kong (living in exile in Canada)

candidates.rationale: Ship captain for Sea-Watch who in 2019 docked a rescue vessel carrying rescued migrants in Lampedusa, Italy, without permission, arguing international maritime law obligated her to bring them to safety.
candidates.objections: Faced Italian criminal charges over the docking incident (later dropped); read by some as a humanitarian hero and by others as having broken the law — state both positions rather than picking one.

candidates.rationale: One of Mexico's most prominent investigative journalists, reporting on government corruption including the 2014 "Casa Blanca" presidential-family real-estate investigation.
candidates.objections: Was fired from her radio program in 2015 in a dispute widely read as retaliation for her reporting; report this as a documented event, not editorialized framing.

candidates.rationale: Pediatrician and former Rwandan Minister of Health credited with major gains in child mortality, HIV treatment access, and health-system rebuilding after the 1994 genocide; now trains health-equity leaders through the University of Global Health Equity.
candidates.objections: Served as a minister under the Kagame government, which has documented, credible human-rights criticisms (political repression, press freedom); her health-policy record and her government affiliation are both worth naming, without treating one as canceling out the other.

candidates.rationale: Former model who became a UN special ambassador against female genital mutilation and founded the Desert Flower Foundation; her memoir "Desert Flower" brought international attention to the issue.
candidates.objections: Some journalists have raised fact-checking questions about specific details/dates in her memoir's account of her early life — a sourcing caution to flag in any profile, not grounds to dismiss the later advocacy work.

candidates.rationale: Researcher and author on human trafficking and forced labor, including "Cobalt Red" (2023), which investigated child and forced labor in Democratic Republic of Congo cobalt mining supplying global battery manufacturers.
candidates.objections: Mining companies named in "Cobalt Red" have publicly disputed specific claims in the book; treat the book's findings as contested, sourced allegations rather than settled fact.

candidates.rationale: Cellist who founded the Silk Road Ensemble to build cultural connection across conflict lines and has performed in settings explicitly framed as reconciliation and cultural diplomacy, including post-conflict regions.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found, but worth an explicit editorial call: he is a celebrated artist rather than a frontline humanitarian case, so his inclusion rests on cultural-diplomacy impact -- flag for Silas whether that counts as this project's kind of case or skews toward Pop-Culture-style inclusion.

candidates.rationale: Founded Cambodian Self Help Demining, a locally-led organization clearing landmines from rural Cambodian villages left over from decades of war.
candidates.objections: As a child he was conscripted first by the Khmer Rouge and later by Vietnamese forces and made to lay some of the same kinds of mines he now clears — an important, already-disclosed complexity in his own biography, not a simple hero narrative, and should be presented that way.

candidates.rationale: Founded Acacias for All, planting drought-resistant acacia trees with Tunisian farming communities to fight desertification while creating rural income.
candidates.objections: No significant controversy found; public sourcing is thinner than for larger international NGOs — verify current organizational status and scale before publishing specific figures.

candidates.rationale: Atmospheric scientist known for communicating climate science to audiences, including evangelical Christian communities, that public climate messaging often fails to reach.
candidates.objections: A frequent target of politically motivated attacks in US climate-policy debates; her explicit framing of climate change through a Christian-evangelical lens is itself sometimes a point of public debate, worth naming rather than smoothing over.

candidates.rationale: Sal Khan began making short math videos to tutor his cousins and turned them into Khan Academy, a nonprofit offering free lessons to anyone with an internet connection. Its courses are used by millions of learners worldwide in dozens of languages.

Savitribai Phule co-founded one of the first schools for girls in India in Pune in 1848 and taught there despite harassment from people who opposed educating girls and lower-caste children. She also ran a shelter for widows and died in 1897 after caring for plague patients.

Jyotirao Phule opened schools for girls and for Dalit children in 1840s Pune, working alongside his wife Savitribai. He founded the Satyashodhak Samaj to challenge caste discrimination and wrote widely against untouchability.

Maria Montessori, one of Italy's first women physicians, opened her Casa dei Bambini in a poor Rome neighbourhood in 1907 and developed a method built on children's self-directed learning. Montessori schools now operate on every inhabited continent.
candidates.objections: She cooperated with Mussolini's government for a period in the 1920s before breaking with it and leaving Italy in 1934.

candidates.rationale: Paulo Freire's literacy campaigns taught Brazilian farm workers to read in weeks by building lessons from their own lives, work that got him jailed and exiled after the 1964 coup. His book Pedagogy of the Oppressed became one of the most cited works in education.

Anne Sullivan, herself partially blind and raised in a poorhouse, became Helen Keller's teacher in 1887 and broke through by spelling words into her hand. She remained Keller's companion and teacher for nearly fifty years.

Mary McLeod Bethune founded a school for Black girls in Daytona Beach in 1904 with a few dollars, which grew into Bethune-Cookman University. She later advised Franklin Roosevelt and founded the National Council of Negro Women.

Bolivian-born Jaime Escalante built a calculus programme at East Los Angeles's Garfield High School that sent hundreds of working-class Latino students to pass the AP exam. His story was told in the film Stand and Deliver.

Marva Collins used her pension savings to open Westside Preparatory School in Chicago in 1975 for children other schools had written off. Her classical, high-expectation teaching drew national attention and was adopted by teachers across the country.

Blinded in a childhood accident, Louis Braille developed the raised-dot reading and writing system as a teenager at the Paris school for blind youth. Braille is still the basis of literacy for blind people worldwide.

Aaron Swartz helped build RSS, Creative Commons licensing tools and Reddit, and campaigned for free access to public knowledge and against the SOPA internet bill. Facing federal prosecution over mass downloads of academic articles, he died in 2013, and his case spurred reform debate.
candidates.objections: His bulk downloading of JSTOR articles was unauthorised, which was the basis of the charges against him.

candidates.rationale: Brewster Kahle founded the Internet Archive in 1996, whose Wayback Machine has preserved hundreds of billions of web pages. The archive also offers millions of free books, recordings and films as a public digital library.
candidates.objections: The Archive's lending of scanned books without publisher permission during 2020 was found to infringe copyright in Hachette v. Internet Archive.

candidates.rationale: Ziauddin Yousafzai founded and ran a school in Swat that taught girls and spoke out publicly when the Taliban banned girls' schooling there. He raised his daughter Malala to speak freely and continues to campaign for girls' education.

Sakena Yacoobi founded the Afghan Institute of Learning in 1995 and ran underground home schools for thousands of girls while the Taliban banned girls' education. Her organisation has reached millions of Afghans with schooling and health training.

Geoffrey Canada built the Harlem Children's Zone, which surrounds children in a 97-block area with schooling, health and family support from birth to college. It became a model for the federal Promise Neighborhoods programme.

Friedrich Fröbel opened the first kindergarten in 1837 in Bad Blankenburg, arguing that young children learn best through structured play. His 'gifts' and play-based approach shaped early childhood education around the world.

Rabindranath Tagore, the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature, founded an open-air school at Santiniketan that grew into Visva-Bharati University. He championed learning rooted in nature, the arts and exchange between cultures.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar opened dozens of schools for girls in Bengal and wrote a Bengali primer still used today. He campaigned successfully for the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856.

Begum Rokeya founded the Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School in Kolkata in 1911 and went door to door persuading families to send daughters. Her feminist utopian story Sultana's Dream is an early classic of science fiction.
Pandita Ramabai, a Sanskrit scholar, founded the Sharada Sadan and Mukti Mission to house and educate widows and famine-stricken girls. She also translated the Bible into Marathi.

When Prudence Crandall admitted a Black student to her Connecticut school in 1832, she turned it into a school for Black girls rather than turn her away. She was arrested under a law passed to stop her and the school was attacked by a mob.

Social studies teacher Christa McAuliffe was selected from more than 11,000 applicants to be the first teacher in space and planned to teach lessons from orbit. She died in the Challenger disaster in 1986, and her lessons were later taught from the ISS in her honour.
Erin Gruwell's Long Beach students, many written off as unteachable, wrote journals about their lives that became The Freedom Writers Diary. Her foundation trains teachers to use the same approach.
LeVar Burton hosted Reading Rainbow for more than two decades, encouraging generations of children to read. He continues to promote reading through his podcast LeVar Burton Reads.
Bill Nye's television show Bill Nye the Science Guy made hands-on science fun for a generation of children in the 1990s. He now leads The Planetary Society and speaks up for science literacy.
Hank Green co-created Crash Course and SciShow, free video series used in classrooms around the world. With his brother John he also co-founded VidCon and the charity project Project for Awesome.

Author John Green co-created the free Crash Course video lessons with his brother Hank. He has since campaigned for cheaper tuberculosis testing and treatment and backs maternal health care in Sierra Leone.

Sonam Wangchuk founded SECMOL to reform schooling in Ladakh, where most students had been failing state exams taught in unfamiliar languages. He also invented the ice stupa for storing winter water and campaigns for the fragile Himalayan environment.

Bunker Roy founded the Barefoot College in Tilonia, Rajasthan, which trains rural people, including grandmothers without formal schooling, as solar engineers and teachers. The model has spread to villages in dozens of countries.

Sugata Mitra's Hole in the Wall experiment put computers in Delhi slum walls and found children taught themselves to use them. The work won the 2013 TED Prize and inspired self-organised learning projects.
candidates.objections: Researchers have questioned how far his self-organised learning results generalise.

candidates.rationale: Ranjitsinh Disale added QR codes to textbooks in his village school in Maharashtra to link students to lessons in their own language, and the idea was adopted statewide. He won the 2020 Global Teacher Prize and shared half the prize money with the other finalists.

Nancie Atwell founded the Center for Teaching and Learning in Maine, a demonstration school where students read dozens of books a year. She won the first Global Teacher Prize in 2015 and gave the prize money to her school.
Hanan Al Hroub, who grew up in a refugee camp, developed play-based teaching to help children traumatised by violence feel safe in school. She won the 2016 Global Teacher Prize.

Maggie MacDonnell taught in Salluit, a fly-in Inuit village in Nunavik troubled by youth suicide, running life-skills and fitness programmes that raised graduation rates. She won the 2017 Global Teacher Prize.

Andria Zafirakou learned basics of many of her London students' languages and redesigned the timetable to keep at-risk children in school. She won the 2018 Global Teacher Prize and founded Artists in Residence.

Kakenya Ntaiya bargained with her Maasai village elders to be allowed to go to college, then returned with a doctorate to open the Kakenya Center for Excellence, a girls' school. Its students commit to avoiding FGM and early marriage.
Ann Cotton founded Camfed in 1993 after learning that poverty, not culture, kept Zimbabwean girls out of school. Camfed has supported millions of girls through school in sub-Saharan Africa.

Blind from early childhood, Taha Hussein became one of the leading Arab writers of the twentieth century. As Egypt's education minister he pushed for free public education, famously calling it as necessary as water and air.

Gabriela Mistral worked for years as a rural schoolteacher and helped reform Mexico's schools and libraries in the 1920s. In 1945 she became the first Latin American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Loris Malaguzzi helped parents rebuild preschools from war ruins in Reggio Emilia after 1945 and developed an approach that treats young children as capable researchers. Reggio-inspired preschools now exist worldwide.

Tsuda Umeko was sent to the United States as a child in 1871 and returned to found one of Japan's first private colleges for women in 1900, now Tsuda University. She pushed for women to study at the same level as men.
As president of Peking University from 1916, Cai Yuanpei opened it to diverse viewpoints and admitted women students. He is remembered as a founder of modern Chinese higher education.

Y. C. James Yen taught Chinese labourers in France to read during World War I, then led a mass education movement in China based on 1,000 basic characters. He later founded the International Institute of Rural Reconstruction in the Philippines.

Ki Hajar Dewantara founded the Taman Siswa schools in 1922 to give Indonesian children education at a time when the colonial system excluded most of them. His birthday is Indonesia's National Education Day.
Kartini opened a school for Javanese girls and wrote letters arguing for women's education and freedom, published after her death at 25. Indonesia celebrates Kartini Day each April.
Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet co-founded the first permanent school for deaf students in the United States in 1817 in Hartford. Gallaudet University is named in his honour.

Septima Clark lost her teaching job for belonging to the NAACP and went on to build Citizenship Schools that taught Black Southerners to read and register to vote. Martin Luther King Jr. called her the mother of the movement.

Myles Horton co-founded the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee, which trained labour and civil rights organisers including Rosa Parks. The school was raided and closed by the state before reopening under a new name.

At six years old, Ruby Bridges walked past screaming crowds with federal marshals to integrate William Frantz Elementary School in 1960. She now runs a foundation promoting tolerance through education.
At 16, Barbara Johns led a student walkout over the conditions at her segregated Virginia high school. The resulting lawsuit became one of the cases combined in Brown v. Board of Education.

Elizabeth Eckford faced a mob alone when she tried to enter Little Rock Central High School in 1957, in an image seen around the world. She and the other eight students integrated the school under federal protection.

Tererai Trent, married young in rural Zimbabwe, buried her written dreams under a rock and went on to earn a doctorate in the United States. She returned to build and rebuild schools in her home community.

Pashtana Durrani founded LEARN Afghanistan, which runs digital learning and teaches girls in secret since the Taliban banned them from secondary school. She speaks publicly for Afghan girls' right to learn.
Matiullah Wesa's PenPath group ran mobile libraries and campaigned village to village for schools in rural Afghanistan. He was detained by the Taliban in 2023 for advocating girls' education.
Aziz Royesh co-founded the Marefat School in Kabul, which educated thousands of girls and boys from the Hazara community. He was a top-ten finalist for the 2016 Global Teacher Prize.

After surviving a gang rape ordered by a village council in 2002, Mukhtaran Mai refused to stay silent and took her attackers to court. She used compensation money to open schools for girls in her village.

As a teenager Humaira Bachal began teaching other children in her Karachi neighbourhood, which grew into the Dream Model Street School serving over a thousand students. She has faced threats for educating girls.

Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti ran schools and adult literacy classes for market women in Abeokuta and led protests that forced the Alake to abdicate over unfair taxes. She was one of Nigeria's great campaigners for women's rights.

Charlotte Maxeke became one of the first Black South African women to earn a university degree and co-founded a school with her husband. She founded the Bantu Women's League and campaigned against pass laws.

Historian Carter G. Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History and launched Negro History Week in 1926, which became Black History Month. His book The Mis-Education of the Negro remains widely read.
Nannie Helen Burroughs founded the National Training School for Women and Girls in Washington in 1909, providing education to Black women. She was also a prominent suffragist and orator.

Anna Julia Cooper, born enslaved, became principal of the M Street High School in Washington and earned a doctorate from the Sorbonne at 66. Her book A Voice from the South is a founding text of Black feminist thought.

Seymour Papert co-created the Logo programming language to let children learn mathematics by programming a turtle. His ideas about learning by making shaped educational technology and inspired LEGO Mindstorms.
Mitchel Resnick's MIT group created Scratch, a free block-based programming language used by tens of millions of children. He promotes playful, creative learning for all kids.

Guatemalan computer scientist Luis von Ahn co-founded Duolingo to make language learning free for people who cannot afford classes. He also invented CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA, which helped digitise books.

Jonathan Kozol's books, from Death at an Early Age to Savage Inequalities, documented how poor and minority children are failed by underfunded schools. He has spent decades advocating for school equity.
Ken Robinson's 2006 TED talk 'Do schools kill creativity?' became the most-watched in TED history. He advised governments on arts and creative education.

Carla Hayden became the first woman and first African American to serve as Librarian of Congress in 2016 and worked to open its collections to the public online. Earlier, she kept Baltimore's libraries open during the 2015 unrest.

Pura Belpré became the New York Public Library's first Puerto Rican librarian and started bilingual story hours for Spanish-speaking children. An award for Latino children's literature is named after her.
Madhav Chavan co-founded Pratham in 1995 to bring education to children in Mumbai's slums, and it grew into one of India's largest education NGOs. He shared the WISE Prize for Education in 2012.
Safeena Husain founded Educate Girls, which works with village volunteers to enrol out-of-school girls in rural India. The organisation received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2025.
Marian Wright Edelman, the first Black woman admitted to the Mississippi bar, founded the Children's Defense Fund in 1973. It has fought for children's health, Head Start and education for decades.

Freeman Hrabowski, jailed as a child marcher in Birmingham in 1963, led the University of Maryland, Baltimore County for three decades. His Meyerhoff Scholars programme became a national model for Black students in science.
Zhang Guimei founded Huaping High School for Girls in Yunnan in 2008, China's first free public high school for girls. Nearly all its graduates have gone to university.
The day after Martin Luther King Jr. was killed, Iowa teacher Jane Elliott ran her 'blue eyes/brown eyes' exercise to teach her pupils about discrimination. She has taught it to audiences ever since.
candidates.objections: Some researchers question the ethics of the exercise's use of humiliation.

candidates.rationale: Ten-year-old Tilly Smith recognised signs of a tsunami from a geography lesson on a Thai beach in 2004 and warned her parents, who helped clear the beach. Around a hundred people are credited as saved.

When al-Shabaab gunmen attacked a bus in Mandera in 2015 and tried to separate Christians from Muslims, teacher Salah Farah and other Muslim passengers refused. He was shot and later died of his wounds.

Johan van Hulst, head of a teacher training college in Amsterdam, helped smuggle hundreds of Jewish children out of a crèche across the street from a deportation centre. He was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.
Andrée Geulen, a young teacher, worked with the Jewish Defence Committee to hide around 300 Jewish children with Belgian families. She kept coded records so they could be reunited after the war.

In 1938-39 Nicholas Winton organised trains that carried 669 mostly Jewish children from Czechoslovakia to safety in Britain, finding foster families for each. He kept quiet about it for nearly fifty years until his scrapbook was found.

Oskar Schindler spent his fortune bribing Nazi officials to keep about 1,200 Jewish workers from death camps, listing them as essential to his factories. He was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations in 1993.
candidates.objections: He joined the Nazi Party, spied for German military intelligence and first profited from confiscated Jewish property and forced labour.

candidates.rationale: Varian Fry ran a rescue network from Marseille in 1940-41 that smuggled around 2,000 refugees, including Marc Chagall and Hannah Arendt, out of Vichy France. He was the first American recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.

Swiss vice-consul Carl Lutz issued protective letters and set up dozens of safe houses in Budapest in 1944, saving tens of thousands of Jews. It is considered one of the largest civilian rescues of the Holocaust.
Italian businessman Giorgio Perlasca posed as Spain's consul in Budapest in 1944 and sheltered thousands of Jews in Spanish-protected houses. He told almost no one about it for decades.
candidates.objections: He had earlier fought for Franco and supported Italian Fascism before turning against it.

candidates.rationale: As Chinese consul-general in Vienna in 1938-40, Ho Feng-Shan issued thousands of visas to Shanghai to Jews trying to escape, against his superior's orders. He was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations in 2000.

Swiss police commander Paul Grüninger backdated papers to let hundreds of Jewish refugees enter Switzerland in 1938 after the border was closed. He was fired and convicted, and cleared only after his death.

Using his cover as a passport officer in Berlin, Frank Foley bent immigration rules to issue visas to thousands of Jews, and even went into camps to get people released. He was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.
Warsaw Zoo director Jan Żabiński smuggled Jews out of the ghetto and hid about 300 people in the zoo's grounds and villa during the occupation. He also fought in the Warsaw Uprising.

Witold Pilecki volunteered to be arrested so he could enter Auschwitz, organise resistance and smuggle out the first detailed reports of the camp. He escaped in 1943 and was executed by Poland's communist regime in 1948.

Polish courier Jan Karski entered the Warsaw Ghetto and a transit camp in disguise, then carried his eyewitness account of the extermination of Jews to Western leaders including Franklin Roosevelt. He later taught at Georgetown for decades.
In 1943 Bulgarian parliament deputy speaker Dimitar Peshev learned of plans to deport Bulgaria's Jews and organised a protest that helped stop it. Around 48,000 Jews in Bulgaria proper survived.
candidates.objections: The same government deported more than 11,000 Jews from Bulgarian-occupied Thrace and Macedonia, which Peshev did not prevent.

candidates.rationale: Pastor André Trocmé led the village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon in sheltering thousands of refugees, many of them Jewish children, during the German occupation. He practised and preached non-violence.
German shipping attaché Georg Duckwitz leaked the plan to deport Denmark's Jews in 1943, allowing nearly all of them to escape to Sweden. He later served as West Germany's ambassador to Denmark.
candidates.objections: He had been a Nazi Party member from the early 1930s.

candidates.rationale: Turkish consul Selahattin Ülkümen insisted to the Germans that Jews on Rhodes were Turkish citizens and saved dozens of them from deportation in 1944. His pregnant wife was fatally injured when German aircraft later bombed the consulate.
Iranian diplomat Abdol Hossein Sardari issued passports to Iranian Jews in occupied Paris and argued to the Nazis that they were not racially Jewish. He is credited with saving many lives.

During the German occupation of Tunisia, Khaled Abdul-Wahab moved Jewish families to his farm to protect them from German soldiers. He is the first Arab nominated for recognition as Righteous Among the Nations.

Defying State Department policy, US vice-consul Hiram Bingham IV issued visas and hid refugees in his home in Marseille in 1940-41, helping thousands escape. In 2002 the American Foreign Service Association posthumously honoured him for constructive dissent.
Corrie ten Boom and her family hid Jews and resisters in a secret room in their Haarlem home. Arrested in 1944, she survived Ravensbrück, where her sister died, and wrote The Hiding Place.
Truus Wijsmuller travelled into Nazi Germany and Austria to arrange the escape of Jewish children, negotiating directly with Adolf Eichmann in Vienna. She helped around 10,000 children reach safety.

Acting Dutch consul Jan Zwartendijk in Kaunas issued thousands of Curaçao destination visas in 1940 that allowed Jews to obtain Chiune Sugihara's transit visas and escape. He was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer helped lead the Confessing Church against Nazi control and helped Jews escape to Switzerland. He was executed at Flossenbürg in April 1945.
candidates.objections: He took part in the conspiracy to assassinate Hitler, which some pacifists regard as inconsistent with his earlier views.

candidates.rationale: Siemens manager John Rabe led the Nanking Safety Zone during the 1937 Japanese massacre, helping protect around 200,000 Chinese civilians. His diaries became key evidence of the atrocities.
candidates.objections: He was a Nazi Party member and appealed to Hitler to intervene.

candidates.rationale: Minnie Vautrin turned Ginling College into a refuge for thousands of women and children during the Nanjing Massacre. Her diary is an important record of the events.
Margit Slachta, the first woman elected to Hungary's parliament, led her Sisters of Social Service in sheltering Jews in Budapest. Her order is credited with saving about 2,000 people.

As a US army sergeant in a German POW camp in 1945, Roddie Edmonds refused an order to identify Jewish prisoners, telling the commandant 'We are all Jews here.' He was the first American soldier recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.
Princess Alice, mother of Prince Philip, hid the Jewish Cohen family in her Athens home during the German occupation. She was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.
Noor Inayat Khan was the first woman radio operator sent into occupied France by Britain's SOE and kept transmitting after her network collapsed. She was executed at Dachau in 1944.
Nancy Wake helped Allied airmen and refugees escape France and later led Resistance fighters for the SOE. The Gestapo nicknamed her the White Mouse.
Josephine Baker gathered intelligence for the French Resistance, carrying messages hidden in her sheet music. She later spoke at the 1963 March on Washington and was admitted to the Panthéon in 2021.
Andrée de Jongh set up the Comet Line, which smuggled hundreds of Allied airmen from Belgium over the Pyrenees to Spain. She crossed the mountains on foot many times before she was captured.
Army helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson Jr. landed between American soldiers and Vietnamese villagers at My Lai in 1968 and evacuated survivors. He testified about the massacre and was shunned for years.
Conscientious objector Desmond Doss refused to carry a weapon but rescued about 75 wounded soldiers at Okinawa in 1945. He received the Medal of Honor.
In 2007 construction worker Wesley Autrey jumped onto New York subway tracks and pinned a man having a seizure between the rails as a train passed over them. Both survived.
Captain Chesley Sullenberger landed US Airways Flight 1549 on the Hudson River in 2009 after both engines failed, and all 155 people aboard survived. He has since advocated for aviation safety.
Holocaust survivor and engineering professor Liviu Librescu blocked his classroom door during the 2007 Virginia Tech shooting, allowing most of his students to escape. He was killed.

In 2018 Malian migrant Mamoudou Gassama climbed four storeys of a Paris building to rescue a child dangling from a balcony. He was granted French citizenship and offered a place with the Paris fire brigade.
British cave diver Rick Stanton was among the first to reach the trapped Thai youth football team in 2018 and helped bring them out. He has taken part in many cave rescues.
John Volanthen found the trapped Wild Boars football team in Tham Luang cave in 2018 and helped carry them out underwater. He also works with Scouts.
Morgan Stanley security director Rick Rescorla had drilled staff for evacuations and got about 2,700 people out of the South Tower on 9/11. He died after going back in.
Franciscan friar Mychal Judge was a New York fire chaplain who ministered to people with AIDS and the homeless. He was killed at the World Trade Center on 9/11.
New York police officer Frank Serpico exposed widespread corruption, leading to the Knapp Commission. He was shot in the face during a raid in 1971.

Military analyst Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers in 1971, revealing that successive governments had misled the public about the Vietnam War. He faced prosecution until the case was dismissed.
US Army reservist Joseph Darby turned over photos of prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib to investigators in 2004. He received threats after being publicly identified.
US Army captain Ian Fishback reported detainee abuse in Iraq and wrote to Senator John McCain, helping lead to the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005. He died in 2021.
Ophthalmologist Li Wenliang warned colleagues about a new SARS-like illness in Wuhan in December 2019 and was reprimanded by police. He died of COVID-19 in February 2020.
Emergency department director Ai Fen circulated a lab report about the new coronavirus in December 2019 and was reprimanded. She later spoke out publicly.
Italian WHO doctor Carlo Urbani identified the SARS outbreak in Hanoi in 2003 and persuaded officials to act quickly. He died of the disease.
Virologist Sheik Humarr Khan led Sierra Leone's fight against Ebola in 2014 and treated more than 100 patients. He died of the disease.
Stella Adadevoh diagnosed the first Ebola case in Lagos in 2014 and kept the patient isolated despite pressure. She died of Ebola, and her action helped contain it.
William Still helped hundreds of enslaved people escape through Philadelphia and kept records of their stories. He published The Underground Rail Road in 1872.
During the 1994 genocide, Zura Karuhimbi hid more than 100 people in her home, scaring off killers by claiming spiritual powers. She was awarded Rwanda's Campaign Against Genocide Medal.
Aid worker Carl Wilkens stayed in Kigali during the 1994 genocide and helped save orphans. He now teaches about the genocide.
Senegalese UN officer Mbaye Diagne smuggled hundreds of people past checkpoints during the Rwandan genocide. He was killed in 1994, and the UN named a medal after him.
General Roméo Dallaire warned the UN of genocide in Rwanda and stayed with a small force that protected thousands. He has since campaigned against child soldiers.
Flight attendant Neerja Bhanot hid passports and helped passengers escape during the 1986 hijacking of Pan Am Flight 73. She was killed shielding children.
Mumbai police officer Tukaram Omble grabbed a gunman's rifle during the 2008 attacks, allowing the attacker to be captured alive. He was killed.
Fifteen-year-old Aitzaz Hasan stopped a suicide bomber approaching his school in 2014. He was killed.
Mother Maria Skobtsova sheltered Jews in Paris and helped children escape. She died at Ravensbrück in 1945.
Grace Darling rowed with her father to rescue survivors of the Forfarshire shipwreck in 1838. She became a national heroine.

In 2015 Sara Mardini and her sister swam alongside a failing dinghy of refugees crossing to Lesbos, helping it reach shore. She returned to Lesbos to volunteer with a search-and-rescue group and was arrested by Greek authorities in 2018 on charges widely condemned by human rights groups.

Yusra Mardini helped keep an overloaded refugee dinghy moving through the Aegean in 2015 by swimming beside it. She went on to swim for the Refugee Olympic Team in 2016 and 2020 and became a UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador.

Pia Klemp captained civilian rescue ships in the Mediterranean that pulled hundreds of migrants from sinking boats. She faced a lengthy Italian investigation over the rescues and turned down a Paris city medal in protest at European migration policy.

One of the first women to fly US Navy fighter jets, Tammie Jo Shults calmly landed Southwest Airlines Flight 1380 in 2018 after an engine exploded and depressurised the cabin. One passenger died and 148 others survived.
In May 1989 Major General Xu Qinxian, commander of the 38th Group Army, refused to lead his troops into Beijing without written orders. He was court-martialled and imprisoned.
Schoolteacher Trevor Chadwick ran the Prague end of the Czech Kindertransport in 1939, negotiating with the Gestapo to get children out. He was posthumously named a British Hero of the Holocaust.

Danish missionary Karen Jeppe worked in Aleppo for the League of Nations rescuing Armenian women and children who had been abducted during the genocide. She helped free well over a thousand and resettle them.
In March 2022, Russian state TV editor Marina Ovsyannikova ran onto a live news broadcast holding a sign against the war in Ukraine. She was prosecuted and fled Russia.

In 2020 Belarusian opposition leader Maria Kalesnikava tore up her passport at the Ukrainian border to stop authorities from expelling her. She was sentenced to 11 years in prison and released in 2025.
Loujain al-Hathloul campaigned for Saudi women's right to drive and against male guardianship laws. She was jailed for nearly three years and has reported torture in detention.

Raed Saleh led the Syria Civil Defence, known as the White Helmets, whose volunteers pulled tens of thousands of people from bombed buildings during the civil war. He became a minister in Syria's post-Assad government in 2025.
In 2013 Antoinette Tuff, a bookkeeper at a Georgia elementary school, calmly talked an armed man into surrendering. No one was hurt.
Yuliia Paievska, known as Taira, led a volunteer medic unit in Mariupol and filmed the siege on a bodycam. She was captured by Russian forces in 2022 and released three months later.
Beyers Naudé, a senior Dutch Reformed minister, broke with his church to oppose apartheid and founded the Christian Institute. He was banned for seven years.
After her son disappeared, Azucena Villaflor founded the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo in 1977. She was abducted and killed by the junta.
During Myanmar's 2021 protests, Catholic nun Ann Rose Nu Tawng knelt before armed police in Myitkyina and begged them not to shoot protesters. Images of her plea circulated worldwide.
Zarifa Ghafari became mayor of Maidan Shahr in 2018 and survived several assassination attempts. Her father was killed in 2020.
Andrew Ng's free Stanford machine-learning course drew over 100,000 students online and led him to co-found Coursera in 2012. He has since taught millions of people through free and low-cost courses.

MIT professor Anant Agarwal taught the first edX course and led edX, the MIT-Harvard platform that offered university courses free online to millions. He won the 2016 Yidan Prize for Education Development.

Linda Darling-Hammond's research on teacher preparation and school funding shaped education policy across the United States. She founded the Learning Policy Institute and received the Yidan Prize in 2022.

Former Afghan women's football captain Khalida Popal helped organise the evacuation of dozens of players and their families after the Taliban took Kabul in 2021. She had earlier exposed abuse of players within the Afghan federation.

Days after Myanmar's 2021 coup, ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun ended a speech at the UN General Assembly with the three-finger salute and called for international action against the military. He kept his seat at the UN despite the junta's attempts to replace him.

Amani Ballour ran an underground hospital in besieged Eastern Ghouta, treating civilians through bombing and chemical attacks. Her work was shown in the documentary The Cave and she received the Council of Europe's Raoul Wallenberg Prize.

Clara Barton nursed wounded soldiers on Civil War battlefields and afterward ran an office that traced tens of thousands of missing soldiers for their families. She founded the American Red Cross in 1881 and led its disaster relief for more than two decades.
candidates.objections: She was pushed out of the Red Cross in 1904 amid criticism of her autocratic, poorly documented management.

candidates.rationale: Italian surgeon Gino Strada co-founded the NGO Emergency in 1994, which built free hospitals for war victims in Afghanistan, Iraq, Sudan, Sierra Leone and elsewhere. It has treated millions of patients, and he campaigned all his life against war and landmines.

Brazilian pediatrician Zilda Arns founded the Pastoral da Criança, a network of volunteer community health workers that taught families simple remedies such as oral rehydration and helped bring down infant mortality across Brazil. She died in the 2010 Haiti earthquake while in Port-au-Prince to share the model.

Sindhutai Sapkal was abandoned as a young mother and survived by begging, then went on to take in and raise more than a thousand orphaned children in Maharashtra. The homes she founded continue that care, and India awarded her the Padma Shri.

Dolores Huerta co-founded the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers, and negotiated contracts that won farmworkers better wages and safer conditions. Her foundation still organizes low-income communities, and 'Sí, se puede' was her slogan.

After his polar expeditions, Fridtjof Nansen brought home hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war for the League of Nations and organized relief during the Russian famine of 1921-22. The 'Nansen passport' gave stateless refugees legal identity, and he received the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize.

Eglantyne Jebb co-founded Save the Children in 1919 to feed children starving under the post-war blockade of Central Europe. She drafted the 1924 Declaration of the Rights of the Child, the forerunner of the UN Convention.

Florence Nightingale reformed military hospital care during the Crimean War and used statistics and pioneering data graphics to show that sanitation saves lives. The nursing school she founded helped make nursing a respected profession.
candidates.objections: Historians note she was slow to accept that her Scutari hospital's own conditions drove its death rate, and her record is sometimes set against Mary Seacole's.

candidates.rationale: Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-Scottish healer, paid her own way to Crimea when British authorities turned her down and set up the British Hotel near the front to feed and nurse soldiers. Once forgotten, she is now celebrated as a pioneer of care across lines of race and empire.

Sadako Ogata led UNHCR from 1991 to 2000 through the Kurdish exodus, the Balkan wars and the Great Lakes crisis, and extended its protection to internally displaced people. She later headed the Japan International Cooperation Agency.

Audrey Hepburn survived wartime hunger in the occupied Netherlands and became one of cinema's best-loved stars. In her last years she made field missions for UNICEF to Ethiopia, Somalia and other crisis zones, drawing world attention to child hunger.

Diana was photographed shaking hands with an AIDS patient in 1987, at a time of deep fear and stigma, and in 1997 she walked through an Angolan minefield to support the campaign against landmines. Her advocacy helped build momentum for the Ottawa mine-ban treaty.

Angelina Jolie served as a UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador and then Special Envoy for two decades, making dozens of field visits to refugee camps from Sierra Leone to Syria. She co-founded the Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict Initiative with UK foreign secretary William Hague.
Bob Geldof organized Band Aid in 1984 and the Live Aid concerts in 1985, raising well over 100 million pounds for famine relief in Ethiopia. He later helped drive the Live 8 campaign for debt relief.
candidates.objections: Critics have argued Band Aid's lyrics and imagery portrayed Africa condescendingly, and some aid money reaching Ethiopia may have been diverted by the regime.

candidates.rationale: After his presidency, Jimmy Carter founded the Carter Center, which monitored elections worldwide and led the campaign that has nearly wiped out Guinea worm disease. For decades he and Rosalynn swung hammers building homes with Habitat for Humanity, and he received the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: His presidency faced criticism over inflation, the Iran hostage crisis and support for some authoritarian allies.

candidates.rationale: Rosalynn Carter spent five decades advocating for people with mental illness, including chairing the President's Commission on Mental Health, and founded an institute supporting family caregivers. She co-founded the Carter Center and volunteered with Habitat for Humanity alongside her husband.

German physician and nun Ruth Pfau devoted more than fifty years to fighting leprosy in Pakistan, building a national network of clinics. The WHO declared leprosy controlled in Pakistan in 1996, and she received a state funeral.

American surgeon Tom Catena has for years been the main doctor at Mother of Mercy Hospital in Sudan's Nuba Mountains, serving hundreds of thousands of people through bombing and blockade. He received the Aurora Prize for Awakening Humanity in 2017.

During Burundi's 1993 civil war, Marguerite Barankitse took in orphaned children from both Hutu and Tutsi families and founded Maison Shalom, which grew to include schools and a hospital. She now continues the work with refugees in Rwanda and received the 2016 Aurora Prize.

Jan Egeland served as UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and coordinated the relief response to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. As head of the Norwegian Refugee Council he has spent years speaking bluntly for displaced people and aid access.

Brazilian diplomat Sérgio Vieira de Mello spent over thirty years with the UN, working on refugee repatriation in Cambodia and leading East Timor's transition to independence. He was killed in the 2003 Canal Hotel bombing in Baghdad, and World Humanitarian Day marks the date.

Kim Phúc is the girl in the 1972 'Napalm Girl' photograph, and she survived severe burns. As an adult in Canada she founded the Kim Foundation International to aid child victims of war, and she serves as a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador.

Peter Kropotkin's 1902 book 'Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution' argued from field observation that cooperation, not only competition, drives survival in nature and in human societies. Its ideas still shape grassroots mutual aid networks today.
candidates.objections: He supported the Allied side in the First World War, which split him from many fellow anarchists.

candidates.rationale: Jane Addams co-founded Hull House in Chicago in 1889, a settlement house offering immigrant neighbors child care, classes, clubs and public health advocacy. She became the first American woman awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, in 1931.

Dorothy Day co-founded the Catholic Worker Movement in 1933, opening houses of hospitality that fed and sheltered poor people in cities across America. She was a lifelong pacifist, jailed repeatedly for civil disobedience.

French-born Peter Maurin co-founded the Catholic Worker Movement with Dorothy Day and set out its program of houses of hospitality, farming communes and roundtable discussions. He lived in voluntary poverty alongside the people the houses served.

Nurse Lillian Wald founded New York's Henry Street Settlement and the Visiting Nurse Service, bringing home health care to immigrant families on the Lower East Side. She coined the term 'public health nurse' and pushed for school nurses and child labor laws.
Octavia Hill managed and improved rented housing for poor London families, pioneering the profession of housing management. She campaigned for green space in cities and co-founded the National Trust.
candidates.objections: She opposed state-funded council housing, favoring charity and private management over public provision.

candidates.rationale: Ela Bhatt founded the Self-Employed Women's Association in 1972, organizing street vendors, home-based workers and laborers into a union with more than a million members, its own cooperative bank and insurance. She was one of The Elders.

Aruna Roy left the civil service to work with rural poor communities in Rajasthan and co-founded the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan. Its public hearings on village spending led to India's Right to Information Act of 2005.

Verghese Kurien built the Amul dairy cooperative and led Operation Flood, which made India the world's largest milk producer while giving millions of small farmers ownership. The cooperative model he championed became a pillar of rural livelihoods.
At his New Lanark mills, Robert Owen cut working hours, refused to employ young children, and opened what is often called Britain's first infant school. His ideas inspired the cooperative movement.
candidates.objections: His New Harmony community in Indiana failed within a few years.

candidates.rationale: As a village mayor during the hunger winter of 1846-47, Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen organized bread and seed for farmers, and he went on to found rural credit cooperatives run by their members. The Raiffeisen model spread worldwide, and UNESCO lists the idea of cooperatives as intangible heritage.

Hermann Schulze-Delitzsch founded the first urban cooperative credit associations for artisans and small traders in 1850s Germany, based on self-help and member ownership. His model, alongside Raiffeisen's, became the basis of the credit union movement.

Saul Alinsky organized Chicago's Back of the Yards neighborhood and founded the Industrial Areas Foundation, which trained generations of community organizers. His 'Rules for Radicals' remains a basic text on building power in poor neighborhoods.
candidates.objections: His confrontational tactics remain politically polarizing.

candidates.rationale: Ella Baker worked behind the scenes for the NAACP and SCLC and mentored the students who founded SNCC in 1960. She insisted that ordinary people could lead their own movements, and that approach shaped grassroots organizing for decades.

Sharecropper Fannie Lou Hamer was beaten for registering Black voters in Mississippi and co-led the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party's challenge in 1964. She also founded the Freedom Farm Cooperative to feed and house poor families of every race.

Grace Lee Boggs spent seven decades organizing in Detroit, and in later life founded Detroit Summer, a youth program for community gardens and neighborhood rebuilding. Her work helped inspire the city's urban farming movement.

Father Greg Boyle founded Homeboy Industries in Los Angeles, which employs and trains former gang members and people coming out of prison, and offers tattoo removal and counseling. It has become the world's largest gang rehabilitation program.

Ai-jen Poo co-founded Domestic Workers United and leads the National Domestic Workers Alliance, which won the first Domestic Workers' Bill of Rights in New York in 2010. She also co-leads Caring Across Generations, which campaigns for a better care system.

Maggie Lena Walker led the Independent Order of St. Luke, a Black mutual aid society in Richmond, Virginia, and in 1903 founded the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank. She was the first woman of any race to charter a bank in the United States, and the bank made home ownership possible for many Black families.

Wilma Mankiller began with self-help projects such as the Bell water-line project, where residents built their own water system, and became the Cherokee Nation's first female Principal Chief in 1985. She expanded tribal health, housing and education programs.

Larry Itliong led Filipino grape workers in the 1965 Delano strike that grew into the historic United Farm Workers grape boycott. He also pushed for Agbayani Village, a retirement home for aging Filipino farmworkers.

Cleve Jones conceived the NAMES Project AIDS Memorial Quilt in 1985. It grew to tens of thousands of panels sewn by friends and families to honor people lost to AIDS and to fight stigma. He co-founded the San Francisco AIDS Foundation.

In 1980s Arkansas, Ruth Coker Burks cared for gay men dying of AIDS whose families had abandoned them, driving them to appointments and finding medicine. When no one would bury them, she buried many in her family's cemetery.
candidates.objections: Journalists have questioned some details of her account, including the number of people she cared for.

candidates.rationale: Marsha P. Johnson was a prominent figure in New York's gay liberation movement after Stonewall and co-founded STAR, which sheltered homeless trans youth. She later cared for people with AIDS as an ACT UP activist.

Sylvia Rivera co-founded Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries with Marsha P. Johnson, opening a house for homeless trans and gender-nonconforming youth. She spent decades fighting for poor queer and trans people to be included in the movement.

Belgian priest Damien De Veuster served the isolated leprosy settlement at Kalaupapa on Molokai for sixteen years, building homes, a church and coffins, until he died of the disease himself. His example changed how the world saw people with leprosy.

Mother Marianne Cope ran hospitals in New York before leading sisters to care for leprosy patients in Hawaii in 1883. She stayed on Molokai for thirty years and cared for Father Damien in his final illness.

As a Paris student in 1833, Frédéric Ozanam co-founded the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul to visit and help poor families in their homes. It grew into a volunteer network active in around 150 countries.

Quaker Elizabeth Fry organized schooling, sewing work and decent conditions for women and children in London's Newgate Prison, and her advocacy helped change how prisoners were treated across Europe. She also set up night shelters for homeless people and a training school for nurses.

Eunice Kennedy Shriver started a summer day camp for children with intellectual disabilities in her own backyard in 1962, and it grew into the Special Olympics, now serving millions of athletes worldwide. She also pushed for federal research on intellectual disability.

Paul Newman co-founded Newman's Own, which gives all its profits to charity, more than half a billion dollars so far. He also founded the Hole in the Wall Gang Camp for seriously ill children, which grew into a global network of free camps.

Entertainer Danny Thomas founded St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis in 1962. It treats children with cancer and never bills their families, and its research has helped raise childhood leukemia survival rates dramatically.

Hall of Famer Roberto Clemente spent his off-seasons on charity work in Latin America. He died in a plane crash on New Year's Eve 1972 while personally escorting relief supplies to earthquake-stricken Nicaragua, and MLB's award for community service bears his name.

Drawing on his own childhood relying on free school meals, Manchester footballer Marcus Rashford campaigned in 2020 until the UK government extended meal vouchers through school holidays. He partnered with FareShare to deliver millions of meals.
