NBA great Dikembe Mutombo put millions of his own money into building the Biamba Marie Mutombo Hospital in Kinshasa, named for his mother. He also served as a global ambassador for the NBA and for health causes.
Senegal forward Sadio Mané funded a school, a hospital and a mosque in his home village of Bambali, choosing to invest his earnings in the community that raised him.

Buddhist nun Cheng Yen founded the Tzu Chi Foundation in 1966 with thirty housewives saving a few cents a day. It grew into one of the largest volunteer relief organizations in the world, running hospitals, recycling programs and disaster response in dozens of countries.

Japanese doctor Tetsu Nakamura treated leprosy and other patients in Pakistan and Afghanistan, then turned to digging wells and irrigation canals because, he said, drought caused more illness than any drug could cure. His canals revived farmland for hundreds of thousands of people, and he was shot and killed in 2019.

Toyohiko Kagawa lived in the slums of Kobe for years and organized labor unions, farmers' unions and consumer cooperatives, including the forerunner of the Co-op Kobe. He was a lifelong pacifist and was jailed for his activism.

Bilquis Edhi ran the Edhi Foundation's maternity homes, orphanages and cradle program with her husband Abdul Sattar Edhi. Through that program, abandoned babies could be left safely and then adopted, and thousands of children found homes.

Akhtar Hameed Khan developed the Comilla model of rural cooperatives in what is now Bangladesh, then founded the Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi. There residents built and financed their own low-cost sewer lines, and the approach was copied across Pakistan.

Architect Perween Rahman directed the Orangi Pilot Project, helping residents of Karachi's informal settlements lay sanitation and secure land records. She was murdered in 2013 while documenting land grabs against the poor.

During Bangladesh's 1971 war, Zafrullah Chowdhury co-founded a field hospital, and he then founded Gonoshasthaya Kendra, a people's health center that trained village paramedics. He also championed the 1982 national drug policy that made essential medicines affordable.

Prakash Amte and his wife Mandakini have run the Lok Biradari Prakalp hospital and school for Madia Gond people in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, since 1973. They also run an animal orphanage there. The couple shared the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2008.

Bhagat Puran Singh founded Pingalwara in Amritsar, a home for destitute, disabled and abandoned people that he began by carrying a disabled child on his back for years. He also wrote and published tirelessly on environmental harm.

Anshu Gupta founded Goonj, which turns urban surplus clothing and materials into a resource that rural communities earn through local development work. Its 'Not Just a Piece of Cloth' program provides low-cost sanitary pads, and it mounts large relief drives after disasters.

Sudha Murty broke barriers as the first female engineer hired at TELCO, and as chair of the Infosys Foundation she funded hospitals, school libraries, toilets and disaster relief across India. She is also a much-loved author of children's books.

American-born Rosamond Carr lived in Rwanda for decades and, at 82, turned her flower plantation into the Imbabazi Orphanage after the 1994 genocide, caring for hundreds of children. She stayed in Rwanda until her death at 94.

Maggie Gobran left a university career to found Stephen's Children, which supports thousands of families in Cairo's garbage-collecting communities through schooling, clinics and home visits. She is often called 'Mama Maggie'.

White Helmets volunteer Khaled Omar Harrah became known worldwide in 2014 for pulling a baby alive from rubble in Aleppo after hours of digging. He was killed in an airstrike in 2016 while carrying out rescues.

Olive farmer Cédric Herrou sheltered and helped hundreds of migrants crossing the Alps from Italy into France's Roya Valley. His prosecution led the French Constitutional Council to recognize the 'principle of fraternity' in 2018.
candidates.objections: He was convicted in lower courts before the fraternity ruling led to his acquittal.

candidates.rationale: As mayor of Riace in Calabria, Domenico Lucano welcomed refugees into the depopulated village, giving them empty homes and work so that the schools and shops could reopen. The 'Riace model' was widely praised as a humane alternative to detention camps.
candidates.objections: He was convicted in 2021 of administrative irregularities with a heavy sentence, largely overturned on appeal in 2023 to a suspended term for a minor offence.

candidates.rationale: Father Luigi Ciotti founded Gruppo Abele in Turin to support people with addictions and other marginalized people. He later founded Libera, which puts land confiscated from the Mafia to social use as cooperatives, and he has lived under police protection because of mafia threats.

Danilo Dolci moved to impoverished western Sicily in 1952. There he led fasts and a 'reverse strike', in which unemployed men repaired a road without pay, to demand jobs and a dam. His nonviolent campaigns against poverty and the Mafia earned him the nickname 'the Sicilian Gandhi'.

Comedian Coluche founded Les Restos du Cœur in 1985 to hand out free meals in winter. It became a permanent charity serving well over a hundred million meals a year, and the 'Coluche law' gave French donors tax relief on gifts to such charities.

Priest Joseph Wresinski, himself raised in poverty, founded ATD Fourth World in a homeless camp at Noisy-le-Grand in 1957. The movement works with people in extreme poverty as partners. His advocacy led to the UN's International Day for the Eradication of Poverty.

Geneviève de Gaulle-Anthonioz survived Ravensbrück concentration camp after resistance work and went on to lead ATD Fourth World in France for over thirty years. She pushed for France's 1998 law against exclusion.

Sister Emmanuelle spent over twenty years living among the zabbaleen rubbish collectors of Cairo. She raised money to build schools, clinics and homes in their communities. She was one of France's most admired public figures.

Journalist Rupert Neudeck chartered the ship Cap Anamur in 1979 to rescue Vietnamese boat people in the South China Sea, saving over ten thousand lives. He later co-founded the Green Helmets relief group.

Anglican priest Chad Varah founded the Samaritans in 1953, offering a telephone to anyone considering suicide. It grew into a volunteer listening service answering millions of calls a year across the UK and Ireland.

Nurse, social worker and physician Cicely Saunders founded St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967, pioneering palliative care that treats 'total pain', physical, emotional and spiritual. Hospices around the world follow her model.

After serving with the Special Operations Executive in the Second World War, Sue Ryder founded a charity caring for concentration camp survivors and later people with disabilities and terminal illness. It still runs hospices and neurological care centers.

Having slept rough himself, John Bird co-founded The Big Issue in 1991, a magazine sold by homeless and vulnerably housed vendors who keep part of the price. The idea spread internationally, and in the House of Lords he champions future generations.

Father Peter McVerry has worked with homeless young people in Dublin since the 1970s, and his Peter McVerry Trust became one of Ireland's largest housing charities. He has been a persistent critic of housing policy failures.

Sister Stanislaus Kennedy founded Focus Ireland in 1985 to support people who are homeless, and later the Immigrant Council of Ireland. Focus Ireland now houses and helps thousands of people each year.

Adi Roche founded Chernobyl Children International in 1991. It brought thousands of children from contaminated areas of Belarus and Ukraine for recuperative stays in Ireland and funded medical programs. She has worked for decades against nuclear harm.

Swedish nurse Elsa Brändström worked with the Red Cross during the First World War to bring food, medicine and clothing to German and Austrian prisoners in Siberian camps. She later founded homes for orphans and helped refugees in the United States.

Astronomer Janina Ochojska founded Polish Humanitarian Action in 1992 and led convoys to besieged Sarajevo. The group went on to drill wells and run relief in Chechnya, South Sudan, Syria and Ukraine, and she was later elected to the European Parliament.

Broadcaster Jerzy Owsiak founded the Great Orchestra of Christmas Charity, whose one-day annual fundraiser has bought equipment for almost every hospital in Poland. His Pol'and'Rock festival has run for decades.

Mathematician Svetlana Gannushkina co-founded the Civic Assistance Committee in 1990 to give legal and practical aid to refugees and forced migrants in Russia, including people from Chechnya. The group kept working despite being branded a 'foreign agent'.

Sociologist Herbert de Souza, known as Betinho, launched Citizens' Action Against Hunger, Poverty and for Life in 1993, a nationwide network of local committees that collected food for millions. He was a hemophiliac who contracted HIV from a blood transfusion and also campaigned for blood safety.

Archbishop Hélder Câmara of Olinda and Recife lived simply, spoke out against Brazil's military dictatorship and backed base communities and housing for favela residents. He famously said: 'When I give food to the poor, they call me a saint. When I ask why they are poor, they call me a communist.'

Jesuit priest Alberto Hurtado founded Hogar de Cristo in 1944 to shelter homeless children and adults in Santiago, driving his green pickup truck to gather people off the streets. It became one of Chile's largest charities.

Father Alejandro Solalinde founded the Hermanos en el Camino shelter in Ixtepec, Oaxaca, in 2007 for Central American migrants riding the freight trains north. He has faced repeated death threats for denouncing kidnappings and abuses against them.

Sister Norma Pimentel directs Catholic Charities of the Rio Grande Valley. Her Humanitarian Respite Center in McAllen, Texas, has welcomed hundreds of thousands of released asylum-seeking families with food, showers and a place to rest.

Argentine-born priest Pedro Opeka founded Akamasoa near a garbage dump in Antananarivo in 1989. It has helped tens of thousands of people build homes, schools and livelihoods, with families working rather than receiving handouts.

Ophelia Dahl co-founded Partners In Health in 1987 with Paul Farmer and others, and she led it for many years as it grew from a clinic in Haiti to a global health organization. She has championed community health workers.

Stephen Lewis served as UN Special Envoy for HIV/AIDS in Africa and drew global attention to the pandemic's toll on women and children. His Stephen Lewis Foundation funds grassroots groups, especially grandmothers raising orphaned grandchildren.

After losing a leg to cancer, Terry Fox ran nearly a marathon a day across Canada in 1980 on an artificial leg, covering 5,373 kilometres before cancer stopped him. Annual Terry Fox Runs have since raised over 850 million dollars for cancer research.

Ophthalmologist Fred Hollows led a national program treating eye disease in Aboriginal communities and worked to make low-cost intraocular lenses so that cataract surgery could be done cheaply in Eritrea and Nepal. The Fred Hollows Foundation has restored sight to millions.

Australian gynecologist Catherine Hamlin and her husband Reginald co-founded the Addis Ababa Fistula Hospital, which has given free surgery to tens of thousands of women. She also founded a midwifery college to prevent fistula in the first place.

Methodist minister Ted Noffs founded the Wayside Chapel in Kings Cross, Sydney, in 1964 as a place of welcome for homeless, addicted and marginalized people. He opened Australia's first drug referral centre and founded what became the Ted Noffs Foundation for young people.

French-born nun Suzanne Aubert worked among Māori communities, wrote a Māori-language prayer book and phrase book, and founded the Sisters of Compassion. They opened New Zealand's first soup kitchen and homes for incurables and foundlings in Wellington.
Efren Peñaflorida and his Dynamic Teen Company brought lessons to children in the streets and slums of Cavite by pushing a cart-classroom. He was named CNN Hero of the Year in 2009.

Prateep Ungsongtham grew up in Bangkok's Klong Toey slum and started a one-baht-a-day school for its children as a teenager. It grew into the Duang Prateep Foundation, which runs schools, health work and community programs, and she won the Ramon Magsaysay Award.

Karen doctor Cynthia Maung fled Myanmar in 1988 and founded the Mae Tao Clinic in Mae Sot, Thailand, giving free care to refugees, migrants and people crossing the border. It sees tens of thousands of patients a year.

Anuradha Koirala founded Maiti Nepal in 1993. It rescues and shelters women and girls trafficked for sexual exploitation and patrols the India border to stop trafficking. She was named CNN Hero of the Year in 2010.

Pushpa Basnet founded the Early Childhood Development Center in Kathmandu to give children who would otherwise live in prison with their parents a home and schooling. She was CNN Hero of the Year in 2012.

Schoolteacher A. T. Ariyaratne founded the Sarvodaya Shramadana Movement in 1958, through which villagers volunteered labor to build roads, wells and schools. It grew into Sri Lanka's largest community development network, active in thousands of villages.

Basque priest José María Arizmendiarrieta founded a technical school in Mondragón in 1943, and his students went on to create the worker cooperatives that became the Mondragon Corporation. It is one of the world's largest worker-owned enterprises.

Journalist Alphonse Desjardins founded the first caisse populaire in Lévis, Quebec, in 1900 to free working families from loan sharks. The Desjardins movement became North America's largest federation of credit unions, and he helped launch the first US credit union.

Priest and educator Moses Coady led the Antigonish Movement in Nova Scotia, helping fishermen and miners form study clubs, credit unions and cooperatives to escape poverty. The Coady International Institute continues this work worldwide.

Elinor Ostrom showed through fieldwork that communities around the world can manage shared forests, fisheries and water sustainably without either privatization or top-down control. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, in 2009.

Jane Jacobs' 1961 book 'The Death and Life of Great American Cities' argued for mixed-use, walkable neighborhoods watched over by their residents. She led fights that stopped expressways from destroying Greenwich Village and parts of Toronto.

Baptist pastor Leon Sullivan founded Opportunities Industrialization Centers in Philadelphia in 1964, which trained hundreds of thousands of people for jobs. His Sullivan Principles pressed US companies operating in apartheid South Africa to treat workers equally.

Irish-born priest Edward Flanagan founded Boys Town in Nebraska in 1917 as a home for homeless and troubled boys of every race and religion. He later campaigned internationally for child welfare reform.

'Mother' Clara Hale cared for more than 40 foster children in her Harlem home, then in 1969 began taking in babies born addicted to drugs, and later babies with HIV. Hale House cared for hundreds of infants, and President Reagan called her a true American hero.

Mitch Snyder led the Community for Creative Non-Violence in Washington, D.C. His fasts and protests won a large federal shelter for homeless people and helped push passage of the McKinney Homeless Assistance Act of 1987.

Duty Free Shoppers co-founder Chuck Feeney secretly gave away about 8 billion dollars through Atlantic Philanthropies to universities, health care, peace in Northern Ireland and human rights. He lived modestly in a rented flat, and his example inspired the 'giving while living' movement.

Since 2019 novelist MacKenzie Scott has given away well over 19 billion dollars, much of it as unrestricted gifts to food banks, community colleges, historically Black colleges and local nonprofits. She trusts the organizations closest to their communities to decide how to use it.

Singer-songwriter Harry Chapin co-founded World Hunger Year, now WhyHunger, and played hundreds of benefit concerts a year. He also lobbied for the presidential commission on world hunger and was posthumously awarded the Congressional Gold Medal.

Chef Alice Waters helped launch the farm-to-table movement at Chez Panisse and in 1995 founded the Edible Schoolyard in Berkeley. There students grow, cook and share food, and the approach has spread to thousands of schools.

Frances Moore Lappé's 1971 bestseller 'Diet for a Small Planet' argued that world hunger comes from how food is distributed and controlled, not from scarcity. She co-founded Food First to research the root causes of hunger.

LeBron James's family foundation opened the I Promise School in his hometown of Akron in 2018 for struggling students. It offers free tuition, meals, bikes and support for families, and he has also funded college scholarships for its students.

Organizer Mariame Kaba founded Project NIA to end youth incarceration in Chicago and has spent decades building community-based alternatives to police and prisons. She teaches mutual aid as practical solidarity.

Lawyer Dean Spade founded the Sylvia Rivera Law Project in 2002 to provide free legal help to low-income trans and gender-nonconforming people. His 2020 book 'Mutual Aid' became a widely used handbook for grassroots support networks.

Kurdish-Turkish immigrant Hamdi Ulukaya founded Chobani and made a point of hiring refugees at his plants, and founded the Tent Partnership for Refugees to get businesses worldwide to do the same. He has pledged most of his wealth to helping refugees.

Christina Noble survived a harsh Dublin childhood in orphanages and homelessness. In 1989 she founded the Christina Noble Children's Foundation, which has helped hundreds of thousands of street and vulnerable children in Vietnam and Mongolia.

Kennedy Odede grew up in Nairobi's Kibera slum and, with a soccer ball and a few cents, started Shining Hope for Communities. It now runs schools for girls, clinics, water points and community programs for millions of urban Kenyans.

Filippo Grandi spent decades in refugee work in Asia, Africa and the Middle East, including leading UNRWA. As UN High Commissioner for Refugees from 2016 to 2025 he led UNHCR through record displacement from Syria, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar.

Josephine Butler led the successful campaign to repeal Britain's Contagious Diseases Acts, which subjected women to forced examinations, and fought child trafficking. She also took destitute and sick women into her own home.

As president he held the Union together through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery through Congress. His Gettysburg and second inaugural addresses remain touchstones for a democracy trying to live up to its promises.
candidates.objections: He long favoured colonising freed Black Americans abroad and approved the hanging of 38 Dakota men in 1862, even while commuting most of the other death sentences.

candidates.rationale: She turned the role of First Lady into a platform for civil rights, labour and refugees, then chaired the UN commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. She pushed that document through to adoption in 1948, and it still anchors international human rights law.
candidates.objections: Letters from her early life contain antisemitic remarks, views she later left behind.

candidates.rationale: As a young SNCC leader he was beaten on the Freedom Rides and on Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday in 1965. He went on to serve Georgia in Congress for 33 years, championing voting rights and urging people to get into 'good trouble'.

In 1977 he became one of the first openly gay people elected to public office in the United States, winning a seat on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. He helped defeat the Briggs Initiative's attempt to fire gay teachers before he was assassinated in 1978, and his call for people to come out still inspires LGBTQ people.
candidates.objections: Biographer Randy Shilts documented that, years before his political career, Milk began a relationship with Jack McKinley when McKinley was 16; the account is a real and recurring objection to his legacy.

candidates.rationale: An anti-apartheid lawyer, he lost an arm to a 1988 car bomb planted by South African security agents in Maputo, then helped shape post-apartheid South Africa's constitution. As a Constitutional Court justice from 1994 to 2009 he wrote the 2005 Fourie judgment that opened the way to same-sex marriage.

As president of Uruguay from 2010 to 2015 he lived on his small farm, gave most of his salary to charity, and oversaw the legalisation of same-sex marriage and cannabis. His plain speaking about consumerism and humility made him a global symbol of politics without vanity.
candidates.objections: In the 1960s and 1970s he was a member of the Tupamaros urban guerrilla movement, which carried out armed robberies and kidnappings.

candidates.rationale: After the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings she led with compassion toward Muslim New Zealanders and passed a ban on military-style semi-automatic weapons within weeks. She also launched the Christchurch Call against online terrorist content and put wellbeing measures at the centre of her government's budgets.
candidates.objections: Critics fault her government for missing its housing and child-poverty targets and for the length of its strict COVID-19 measures.

candidates.rationale: Ireland's first woman president (1990 to 1997), she widened the office's reach to emigrants, marginalised communities and LGBT rights campaigners. As UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and later chair of The Elders, she became a leading voice for climate justice.
candidates.objections: She was criticised for her handling of the 2001 Durban anti-racism conference, where an NGO forum produced antisemitic material.

candidates.rationale: Africa's first elected woman head of state, she led Liberia from 2006 to 2018 after its civil wars, cutting foreign debt and keeping the peace. She shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize for her non-violent work for women's safety and rights, and she received the Ibrahim Prize for her peaceful handover of power.
candidates.objections: She gave early financial support to Charles Taylor, which led Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission to recommend she be barred from office, and she was criticised for appointing her sons to senior posts.

candidates.rationale: As UN Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006 he launched the Millennium Development Goals and the Global Fund, and he championed the Responsibility to Protect principle. He shared the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize and later mediated the end of Kenya's 2008 post-election violence.
candidates.objections: He headed UN peacekeeping during the failures in Rwanda in 1994 and Srebrenica in 1995, and the Oil-for-Food scandal clouded his tenure.

candidates.rationale: As UN Secretary-General he created the first large UN peacekeeping force during the 1956 Suez crisis and defended the organisation's independence from the great powers. He died in a 1961 plane crash while on a peace mission to the Congo and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize after his death.

He negotiated the 1949 armistice agreements between Israel and its Arab neighbours, which in 1950 made him the first African American to win the Nobel Peace Prize. He went on to guide decolonisation and peacekeeping at the UN, and he marched at Selma.

His Ostpolitik eased Cold War tensions with Eastern Europe, and his spontaneous kneeling at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial in 1970 became an icon of German atonement. He received the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize and later chaired the Brandt Commission on global poverty.
candidates.objections: His government issued the 1972 Radikalenerlass, which barred people deemed political radicals from public-sector jobs.

candidates.rationale: As Sweden's prime minister he expanded the welfare state and spoke out against the Vietnam War, apartheid and Franco's Spain. He led the Independent Commission on Disarmament and Security Issues before he was assassinated in Stockholm in 1986.
candidates.objections: The 1973 IB affair revealed a secret intelligence bureau with ties to his Social Democrats that had spied on left-wing Swedes.

candidates.rationale: A Radical Republican leader in the House, he fought slavery and then pushed for full citizenship and equal protection for freed people, shaping the Fourteenth Amendment. He chose to be buried in an integrated cemetery so that his grave would declare 'equality of man before his Creator'.

A fierce anti-slavery senator, he was beaten nearly to death at his desk by Congressman Preston Brooks in 1856 after a speech against slavery's spread. He returned to champion equal rights for freed people and pressed for the civil rights bill that passed as the Civil Rights Act of 1875.

For about twenty years he led the parliamentary campaign that produced the Slave Trade Act of 1807, which banned the British slave trade. He kept pressing for abolition until the Slavery Abolition Act passed days before his death in 1833.
candidates.objections: He backed repressive laws against radicals and trade unions in the 1790s, and for decades he favoured gradual rather than immediate emancipation.

candidates.rationale: As US Secretary of Labor from 1933 to 1945, the first woman to serve in a US cabinet, she drove Social Security, the minimum wage and the forty-hour week. She came into public life after witnessing the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire.

In 1968 she became the first Black woman elected to the US Congress, and in 1972 she became the first Black candidate to seek a major party's presidential nomination. 'Unbought and unbossed', she fought for school meals, the poor and women's rights.

She was the first Black woman elected to Congress from the South, and her 1974 statement during the Watergate impeachment hearings became a classic defence of the Constitution. In Congress she worked to extend the Voting Rights Act to language minorities.
candidates.objections: As chair of the US Commission on Immigration Reform she recommended lowering legal immigration levels, a stance restrictionists later cited.

candidates.rationale: The first woman to serve in both houses of Congress, she delivered her 1950 'Declaration of Conscience' against McCarthyism at a time when few colleagues dared to. She served Maine for more than three decades and was known for her independence.

Elected in 1916, four years before national women's suffrage, she was the first woman in Congress. She voted against US entry into both world wars and was the only member to vote against war after Pearl Harbor, and she was still leading anti-war marches in 1968.

In 1989 this Solidarity adviser became the first non-communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc, steering Poland's peaceful transition to democracy. As UN Special Rapporteur on the former Yugoslavia, he resigned in 1995 in protest at the world's failure to prevent the Srebrenica massacre.

He survived a 1973 kidnapping and a 1980 death sentence under military rule, and he became South Korea's president in 1998. His Sunshine Policy produced the first inter-Korean summit in 2000 and won him the Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: It later emerged that Hyundai had made secret payments to North Korea ahead of the 2000 summit.

candidates.rationale: After her husband's assassination she led the 1986 People Power Revolution that peacefully ousted Ferdinand Marcos. As president she restored democratic institutions under the 1987 constitution, and in 1992 she handed over power rather than seek another term.
candidates.objections: Troops killed protesting farmers in the 1987 Mendiola massacre under her government, and her land reform let her family's Hacienda Luisita avoid redistribution.

candidates.rationale: Exiled by Britain for marrying Ruth Williams, a white Englishwoman, he returned to lead Botswana to independence as a non-racial multiparty democracy. As its first president he invested the country's diamond wealth in schools, roads and health care.

As Botswana's president from 1980 to 1998 he sustained its democracy and its prudent use of diamond revenue, and he stepped down voluntarily. He later facilitated the Inter-Congolese Dialogue and chaired the international panel on the Rwandan genocide.

As president from 1998 to 2008 he led one of Africa's first free national antiretroviral programmes at the height of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, and he publicly took an HIV test himself. He left office on schedule and won the Ibrahim Prize for Achievement in African Leadership in 2008.
candidates.objections: His government was criticised for removing San (Basarwa) communities from the Central Kalahari Game Reserve.

candidates.rationale: As president of Cape Verde from 2001 to 2011 he helped consolidate one of Africa's most stable democracies and stepped down at the end of his term limit. His record won him the 2011 Ibrahim Prize for Achievement in African Leadership.
candidates.objections: He had earlier served as prime minister in Cape Verde's one-party state from 1975 to 1991.

candidates.rationale: After two decades as president he conceded defeat in Senegal's 2000 election and handed power to Abdoulaye Wade, a rare peaceful transfer in the region at the time. He then served as Secretary General of the Francophonie.
candidates.objections: His long rule saw little progress in ending the Casamance conflict.

candidates.rationale: A survivor of detention and torture under Pinochet, she became Chile's first woman president and expanded pensions, early education and reproductive rights. She was also the first head of UN Women and later served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
candidates.objections: Human rights groups criticised her 2022 visit to Xinjiang as too soft on China.

candidates.rationale: As premier of Saskatchewan he introduced North America's first single-payer public hospital and medical insurance, which became the model for Canadian medicare. In 2004 Canadians voted him the 'Greatest Canadian'.
candidates.objections: His 1933 master's thesis endorsed eugenic measures, views he later rejected.

candidates.rationale: He won the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize for proposing the UN Emergency Force that ended the fighting in the Suez crisis. As prime minister he brought in universal health care, the Canada Pension Plan and the maple leaf flag.
candidates.objections: His government accepted US nuclear warheads on Canadian soil in 1963, reversing his earlier opposition.

candidates.rationale: The son of a Welsh coal miner, he became Health Minister and in 1948 founded the National Health Service, care free at the point of use for everyone. He also led a major post-war council housing programme.

Before entering Parliament she worked for Oxfam and campaigners against modern slavery, and as an MP she championed Syrian refugees. She was murdered by a far-right extremist in 2016, and her maiden-speech line 'we have far more in common than that which divides us' inspired the Great Get Together.

As Northern Ireland Secretary from 1997 to 1999 she helped secure the Good Friday Agreement. She famously went into the Maze prison to persuade loyalist prisoners to back the talks. She did this while being treated for a brain tumour.

A civil rights activist turned SDLP leader, he argued for decades that the conflict in Northern Ireland could only be ended by agreement and non-violence. He shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize for his role in bringing about the Good Friday Agreement.

An independent MP, she campaigned for decades for the Family Allowances Act 1945, which paid child benefit directly to mothers. In the 1930s and 1940s she tirelessly lobbied for refugees fleeing Nazism.
candidates.objections: Her writing on Indian child marriage has been criticised as paternalistic.

candidates.rationale: She served as Finland's first woman president from 2000 to 2012 after a long career advocating for human rights, sexual minorities and gender equality. She co-chaired the UN High-level Panel on Global Sustainability.
He led the UN mission that brought Namibia to independence and mediated the 2005 Aceh peace agreement. He also shaped the settlement for Kosovo, and he won the 2008 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Serbia and Russia rejected his Kosovo plan as biased toward independence.

candidates.rationale: Norway's first woman prime minister, she chaired the commission whose 1987 report 'Our Common Future' defined sustainable development. As Director-General of the WHO she led the global tobacco-control treaty.

In 1980 Icelanders made her the world's first democratically elected woman president, a year after she was a single mother known for her work in theatre. Over sixteen years in office she championed the Icelandic language, reforestation and girls' ambitions.

In 2009 she became the world's first openly lesbian head of government, leading Iceland after its banking collapse. Her government legalised same-sex marriage in 2010, and she married her partner under the new law.

A physicist from East Germany, she led Germany steadily for sixteen years through financial, euro and pandemic crises. In 2015 she kept the borders open to more than a million refugees under the motto 'Wir schaffen das' ('We can do this').
candidates.objections: Critics fault her for deepening Germany's dependence on Russian gas through Nord Stream 2 and for pressing harsh austerity on Greece.

candidates.rationale: A survivor of Auschwitz, she legalised abortion in France as health minister in 1975, defending the law against vicious abuse in parliament. In 1979 she became the first president of the directly elected European Parliament.

As France's justice minister he won the abolition of the death penalty in 1981 and ended the discriminatory age of consent for gay men in 1982. He spent the rest of his life campaigning for worldwide abolition.

As President of Ireland from 1997 to 2011, with 'building bridges' as her theme, she reached out to unionist communities in Northern Ireland and hosted Queen Elizabeth II's historic 2011 state visit. She is an outspoken advocate for LGBT people within the Catholic Church.
candidates.objections: In 2005 she apologised for remarks comparing the teaching of hatred toward Catholics in Northern Ireland to Nazi-era hatred of Jews.

candidates.rationale: For 24 years in exile he was the diplomatic voice of East Timor's resistance to Indonesian occupation, and he shared the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize. He later served as Timor-Leste's president and survived being shot in a 2008 assassination attempt.

Born into a caste treated as 'untouchable', he earned doctorates abroad and became chair of the committee that drafted India's constitution, which abolished untouchability. He spent his life fighting caste discrimination.

Born to a boat-owning family in Rameswaram, he became an aerospace scientist and served as India's president from 2002 to 2007. His warmth toward students earned him the name 'People's President', and he died while giving a lecture.
candidates.objections: He was central to India's missile programme and its 1998 nuclear weapons tests.

candidates.rationale: As finance minister in 1991 he opened India's economy, and his reforms lifted millions out of poverty. As prime minister from 2004 to 2014 he enacted the Right to Information Act and a rural employment guarantee, and he was known for his personal integrity.
candidates.objections: His government was dogged by major corruption scandals, such as the 2G spectrum case, though he was not accused of enriching himself.

candidates.rationale: After the 2010 uprising she led Kyrgyzstan's interim government, organised a new parliamentary constitution, and stepped down in 2011 as she had promised. That made her the first woman head of state in Central Asia and a rare voluntary transfer of power in the region.
candidates.objections: The deadly 2010 ethnic violence in Osh happened under her interim government.

candidates.rationale: As a lawyer she won a fourteen-year fight against an illegal landfill in Pezinok, which earned her the Goldman Environmental Prize. She was elected Slovakia's first woman president in 2019 on an anti-corruption platform after the murder of journalist Ján Kuciak.

A teacher and mother, she ran for president in 2020 in place of her jailed husband and drew enormous peaceful crowds against Alexander Lukashenko. She has led the democratic Belarusian opposition from exile ever since.

For thirteen years she was the only Progressive Party MP in South Africa's all-white parliament, using her questions to expose apartheid abuses. She visited Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners on Robben Island to press for better conditions.
candidates.objections: She opposed international economic sanctions against apartheid South Africa.

candidates.rationale: As South Africa's Public Protector from 2009 to 2016 she investigated the powerful without fear. Her Nkandla report led the Constitutional Court to order President Zuma to repay public money, and her 'State of Capture' report exposed corruption.

A citizen of Laguna Pueblo, she became the first Native American cabinet secretary as Secretary of the Interior from 2021 to 2025. She launched the Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative to document the abuses of the boarding-school system.
candidates.objections: Oil and gas interests opposed her restrictions on leasing on federal lands.

candidates.rationale: In 1965 she became the first woman of colour elected to the US Congress. She co-authored Title IX, which banned sex discrimination in federally funded education and transformed women's sports and schooling.

Interned as a child during World War II, he later helped pass the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, which apologised and paid reparations to Japanese Americans. As Transportation Secretary on 9/11 he grounded all flights and then barred airlines from racial profiling of Arab and Muslim passengers.

After his presidency he returned to the House, where he fought for years against the 'gag rule' that silenced anti-slavery petitions. He argued the Amistad case before the Supreme Court in 1841 and won freedom for the Africans who had rebelled aboard the ship.
candidates.objections: As Secretary of State he defended Andrew Jackson's 1818 invasion of Spanish Florida.

candidates.rationale: In 1862 he freed himself, his family and other enslaved people by piloting the Confederate ship Planter out of Charleston Harbor to the Union fleet. He later served five terms in Congress and fought disenfranchisement at South Carolina's 1895 constitutional convention.
In 1971 he became the first Aboriginal Australian to sit in the federal parliament, serving as a senator for Queensland. He crossed the floor dozens of times on principle, often on Indigenous issues.

As president of Kiribati from 2003 to 2016 he made the survival of low-lying island nations a global cause and created the vast Phoenix Islands Protected Area. He planned 'migration with dignity' for his people.

As a boy he witnessed the flash of the 1954 Castle Bravo nuclear test. As foreign minister he sued the nuclear powers at the International Court of Justice and built the 'High Ambition Coalition' that helped secure the 1.5°C goal in the Paris Agreement.
A former prisoner of conscience, he became the Maldives' first democratically elected president in 2008. He held an underwater cabinet meeting in 2009 to dramatise the threat of rising seas.
candidates.objections: In 2012 he ordered the military to detain the chief judge of the Criminal Court, which set off the crisis that ended his presidency.

candidates.rationale: After Costa Rica's 1948 civil war his junta abolished the army, gave women the vote, and set up the institutions of one of Latin America's steadiest democracies. He later won two elected terms as president.
candidates.objections: He came to power by leading the armed uprising of 1948 and ruled by junta for eighteen months.

candidates.rationale: A Black bisexual woman raised in the Maré favela, she was elected to Rio de Janeiro's city council in 2016 and denounced police killings and militias. She was assassinated in 2018, and she has become a worldwide symbol of the fight for justice.

Taiwan's first woman president, she served two terms from 2016 to 2024, and in 2019 her government made Taiwan the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage. She formally apologised to Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2016.

A former legal-aid lawyer for the rural poor, she served as vice president of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022. She criticised the killings in the drug war and ran volunteer-driven pandemic relief on a tiny budget.

A senator jailed without charge for two years under Marcos's martial law, he went on to found the Free Legal Assistance Group, which defended victims of the dictatorship at no cost. He led the Philippine human rights movement until his death in 1987.

In 1990 she defeated Daniel Ortega and became the first woman elected head of state in the Americas. She ended the Contra war, abolished conscription and shrank the army, and she handed power on peacefully in 1997.
candidates.objections: Her market reforms brought painful austerity for many poor Nicaraguans.

candidates.rationale: Imprisoned after the 1956 revolution, he translated literature during his years of silence. He became Hungary's first freely elected president after communism, a much-loved moral figure above party politics.

A writer and documentary filmmaker who kept Estonian culture alive under Soviet rule, he became independent Estonia's president from 1992 to 2001. He helped bring about the withdrawal of Russian troops and anchored the country in Europe.

A music professor, he led the Sąjūdis movement and chaired the parliament that declared Lithuania's independence from the Soviet Union in March 1990. He held firm, without violence, through the Soviet crackdown of January 1991.

Imprisoned and exiled under Mussolini, he fought in the Resistance, and as President of Italy from 1978 to 1985 he became the most popular holder of the office. He was known for his directness and his compassion toward victims of disasters.
A historian and archaeologist, he became Mali's first democratically elected president in 1992 and stepped down after two terms. He later chaired the African Union Commission.
candidates.objections: The 1997 election that re-elected him was boycotted by much of the opposition.

candidates.rationale: Sentenced with Mandela at the Rivonia Trial, he spent 26 years in prison, many on Robben Island. After his release he served in the democratic parliament and founded a foundation to fight racism.

A bomber pilot in World War II, he became a leading voice against the Vietnam War and directed the US Food for Peace programme. With Bob Dole he created the McGovern–Dole school feeding programme, which has fed millions of children.

With Sam Nunn he wrote the 1991 Nunn–Lugar programme, which helped deactivate thousands of former Soviet nuclear warheads and secure dangerous materials. He was respected across party lines for his foreign-policy expertise.

She led the Japanese women's suffrage movement for decades, and after women won the vote she served five terms in the House of Councillors. She was known for clean-election campaigns that refused corporate money.
candidates.objections: She cooperated with wartime government organisations, and she was purged by the occupation authorities from 1947 to 1950.

candidates.rationale: A sociologist and diplomat, she became Sweden's first minister of disarmament and pushed the superpowers at Geneva for decades. She shared the 1982 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: Her 1934 book with Gunnar Myrdal supported Sweden's sterilisation policies.

candidates.rationale: A Wiradjuri teacher, she became the first Aboriginal woman elected to Australia's House of Representatives in 2016. As Minister for Indigenous Australians she led the campaign for a constitutional Indigenous Voice to Parliament.
As Barbados's first woman prime minister she led the country to become a republic in 2021. Her Bridgetown Initiative has pushed global lenders to reform climate finance for vulnerable nations.

An economist elected Moldova's first woman president in 2020, she campaigned against entrenched corruption and steered the country toward EU membership. She has kept it on that course despite heavy Russian interference.
candidates.objections: Critics say her government has restricted pro-Russian parties and media outlets.

candidates.rationale: As prime minister from 1999 to 2008 she introduced civil unions and interest-free student loans, and she upheld New Zealand's nuclear-free stance. She then led the UN Development Programme as its first woman administrator.
candidates.objections: Her government's Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 was widely opposed by Māori as a confiscation of customary rights.

candidates.rationale: As Georgia House minority leader and a voting rights organiser, she built groups that registered hundreds of thousands of new voters. That work helped transform turnout in the state.
candidates.objections: She declined to formally concede the 2018 Georgia governor's race.

candidates.rationale: In 1998 she became the first openly lesbian person elected to Congress, and in 2012 she became the first openly gay US senator. She led passage of the Respect for Marriage Act in 2022.

The first woman to serve as President of the Swiss Confederation, she introduced universal health insurance and pioneered evidence-based drug policy. She later chaired the Global Commission on Drug Policy.

In 1988 he pointed at the camera on live television and challenged Pinochet by name, a moment of courage that helped end the dictatorship. As president from 2000 to 2006 he removed authoritarian provisions from the constitution.

He survived poisonings in 2015 and 2017, then returned to Russia and was sentenced to 25 years for denouncing the war in Ukraine. He was freed in the 2024 prisoner exchange and continues to campaign for Russian political prisoners.
A Moscow municipal deputy, he chose to stay in Russia and was jailed for eight and a half years for speaking about the killings in Bucha. He was freed in the 2024 prisoner exchange.
A leader of the 2014 Umbrella Movement, he became Hong Kong's youngest-ever legislator in 2016 before being disqualified. He now advocates from exile for Hong Kong's freedoms.

A barrister and founding chairman of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, he spent decades defending the rule of law and the city's freedoms. In 2021, in his eighties, he was convicted for joining a peaceful 2019 protest march.

He led the campaign that saved Tasmania's Franklin River from damming in the early 1980s and founded the Australian Greens. As a senator he was the first openly gay member of the Australian parliament.
As Cambodia's Minister of Women's Affairs she campaigned against sex trafficking and domestic violence. She later became an opposition leader and has continued working for democracy from exile.

Her 1889 anti-war novel 'Lay Down Your Arms!' became a bestseller and a manifesto for the peace movement. She encouraged Alfred Nobel to create a peace prize and in 1905 became the first woman to win it.
Fired from Wellesley College for opposing US entry into World War I, she helped lead the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom for decades. She won the 1946 Nobel Peace Prize.

After winning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, he gathered thousands of scientists' signatures against atmospheric nuclear testing, work that helped lead to the 1963 test-ban treaty. That campaign won him a second, unshared Nobel Prize, for peace.
candidates.objections: In later life he promoted megadoses of vitamin C with claims that the evidence did not support.

candidates.rationale: He was the only scientist to leave the Manhattan Project on grounds of conscience. He went on to co-found the Pugwash Conferences to reduce nuclear danger, and in 1995 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Pugwash.

As editor of Die Weltbühne he exposed Germany's secret rearmament and was imprisoned for it. He was then sent to Nazi concentration camps, where he won the 1935 Nobel Peace Prize while still a prisoner, and he died in custody in 1938.
A sculptor and architect, he coordinated the non-violent human rights network Servicio Paz y Justicia across Latin America and was tortured under Argentina's junta. He won the 1980 Nobel Peace Prize.
candidates.objections: He has been criticised for defending the governments of Cuba and Venezuela.

candidates.rationale: After three children were killed in Belfast in 1976, she co-founded the Community of Peace People, which drew tens of thousands onto the streets against sectarian violence. She shared the 1976 Nobel Peace Prize.

As executive director of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, she helped win the 2017 UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. That work brought ICAN the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize.
Jailed repeatedly for campaigning against the death penalty and the oppression of women in Iran, she keeps organising and writing from prison. She won the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize.
He helped broker the 1989 Taif Agreement that ended Lebanon's civil war and led the UN's work on Afghanistan's post-2001 transition. His 2000 Brahimi Report reshaped UN peacekeeping.

As Executive Secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change from 2010 to 2016, she rebuilt global climate talks after the failure in Copenhagen. She steered nearly 200 nations to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
As head of the International Atomic Energy Agency he disputed claims that Iraq had revived its nuclear programme before the 2003 invasion. He shared the 2005 Nobel Peace Prize with the IAEA.
candidates.objections: In 2013 he briefly served as vice president in the military-backed government, then resigned over the Rabaa massacre.

candidates.rationale: As chief UN weapons inspector in 2002 and 2003 he reported finding no evidence of Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and asked for more time before any war. He later chaired the international Weapons of Mass Destruction Commission.
candidates.objections: The IAEA he earlier led failed to detect Iraq's pre-1991 nuclear weapons programme.

candidates.rationale: In 1945 he negotiated the White Buses operation, which brought thousands of prisoners out of Nazi concentration camps to Sweden. As the first UN mediator in Palestine he was assassinated by the Lehi militia in 1948.
candidates.objections: Some historians have alleged that he favoured Scandinavian prisoners over Jewish ones, a charge others dispute.

candidates.rationale: A Polish-Jewish lawyer who lost most of his family in the Holocaust, he coined the word 'genocide'. He campaigned almost single-handedly for the 1948 Genocide Convention.

A jurist and Free French leader, he was a principal drafter of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and later presided over the European Court of Human Rights. He received the 1968 Nobel Peace Prize.

A member of India's Constituent Assembly, she served on the UN commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. There she won the change from 'all men are born free and equal' to 'all human beings'.

A playwright, educator and diplomat, he was vice-chair of the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. He argued that the declaration should draw on many cultures, not the West alone.

At 27 he was chief prosecutor in the Nuremberg trial of Einsatzgruppen commanders, a case that convicted 22 men for the murder of more than a million people. He then spent decades campaigning for the International Criminal Court and 'law not war'.

As chief prosecutor of the Yugoslavia and Rwanda tribunals she indicted Slobodan Milošević, the first sitting head of state charged by an international court. She later served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

A Jordanian diplomat, he helped create the International Criminal Court and wrote a landmark UN report on sexual abuse by peacekeepers. As High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2014 to 2018 he criticised abusers regardless of their power.

After helping design the Soviet hydrogen bomb, he turned against nuclear testing and became the Soviet Union's leading human rights dissident. He won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize and was exiled to Gorky.
candidates.objections: His early career was devoted to building thermonuclear weapons.

candidates.rationale: An Olympic silver medallist and Labour MP, he helped draft the League of Nations Covenant and the UN Charter and campaigned for disarmament throughout his life. He won the 1959 Nobel Peace Prize.
The Mexican diplomat was the driving force behind the 1967 Treaty of Tlatelolco, which made Latin America the first populated nuclear-weapon-free zone. He shared the 1982 Nobel Peace Prize.
A Zulu chief deposed for refusing to quit the ANC, he led its non-violent campaigns against apartheid as president general. In 1960 he became the first African to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

In 1968, as a student, he founded the Community of Sant'Egidio, which serves the poor and brokered the 1992 Rome accords that ended Mozambique's civil war. Sant'Egidio also runs humanitarian corridors for refugees.

A Ugandan minister, she went into the bush in 1994 to meet Joseph Kony and returned in 2004 and 2005 to lead the first direct talks with the Lord's Resistance Army. Those talks laid groundwork for later peace negotiations.

In the 1990s she helped found the Wajir Peace and Development Committee, which ended clan violence in north-eastern Kenya and became a model for peacebuilding across Africa. She won the Right Livelihood Award in 2007.

She co-founded the Northern Ireland Women's Coalition, which won seats at the peace talks and helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement. She later served as Chief Commissioner of the Northern Ireland Human Rights Commission.

A Harvard law professor, he co-founded the Harvard Negotiation Project and co-wrote 'Getting to Yes' (1981), which taught millions to negotiate on interests rather than positions. He advised peacemakers, including in the Camp David talks.

A sociologist, she helped create the academic field of peace research and co-founded the International Peace Research Association. She championed a 'culture of peace' built in families and communities.
His studies of non-violent action, including 'From Dictatorship to Democracy', were translated into dozens of languages. Democracy movements from Serbia to Myanmar used them as practical handbooks.

A minister and labour organiser, he led the Fellowship of Reconciliation and mentored civil rights activists, including Bayard Rustin and James Lawson. He stayed a leading voice against the Vietnam War until his death in 1967.

She founded Oxford Research Group to open dialogue between nuclear-weapons policymakers and their critics, and later Peace Direct to support local peacebuilders. She has been nominated three times for the Nobel Peace Prize.

In 1901 she exposed the deadly conditions in British concentration camps for Boer and Black African civilians, and public outrage led to reforms. She later organised relief for starving families after both the Boer War and World War I.

A Brazilian zoologist, suffragist and federal deputy, she led the push at the 1945 San Francisco conference to write equal rights for women into the UN Charter. She also helped win women the vote in Brazil.

As editor of the Saturday Review he campaigned against nuclear testing and brought the 'Hiroshima Maidens' to the US for reconstructive surgery. He also acted as a back channel between Kennedy, Khrushchev and Pope John XXIII before the 1963 test-ban treaty.

He was the UN's first Emergency Relief Coordinator, mediated between Iran and Iraq and in Darfur, and served as UN Deputy Secretary-General. He later chaired the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
As UN Secretary-General he negotiated the 1988 ceasefire in the Iran–Iraq War. He also oversaw the talks that ended El Salvador's civil war in 1992.
The Burmese teacher and diplomat became UN Secretary-General in 1961 and mediated between Kennedy and Khrushchev during the Cuban Missile Crisis. He was the first person from Asia to hold the post.
candidates.objections: He was criticised for withdrawing UN peacekeepers from Sinai at Egypt's request in 1967, shortly before the Six-Day War.

candidates.rationale: A World War II veteran who was among the first British officers to enter Bergen-Belsen, he worked with Hammarskjöld to build UN peacekeeping. He directed operations for decades and later wrote about UN reform.

As UN Secretary-General from 2007 to 2016 he made climate change a priority, helping to deliver the Paris Agreement, and championed the Sustainable Development Goals. He also spoke up for LGBT rights at the UN.
candidates.objections: An internal UN review found the organisation failed civilians at the end of Sri Lanka's civil war in 2009, and the UN was slow to accept responsibility for Haiti's cholera outbreak.

candidates.rationale: After serving as prime minister of Portugal, he led the UN refugee agency through the Syrian crisis. As UN Secretary-General since 2017 he has pressed for ceasefires and climate action.
candidates.objections: Governments on several sides have accused him of bias in his statements on the Gaza and Ukraine wars.

candidates.rationale: He founded the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue, brokered the 2018 Stockholm Agreement on Yemen as UN envoy, and served as UN Emergency Relief Coordinator. In that role he negotiated the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative.

With her sister Asma Jahangir she co-founded Pakistan's first all-women law firm and its independent Human Rights Commission. She served as the UN's first Special Representative on Human Rights Defenders and is a member of The Elders.

Beyond decades of beloved film work, he has spent years quietly supporting children's hospitals and cancer research through a private foundation he chose not to put his name on. Crew members and strangers have documented so many small, unpublicised kindnesses that his decency has become a genuine cultural touchstone.

Across seven decades of programmes from Life on Earth to Blue Planet II, he brought the living world into billions of homes with patience and wonder. In later life he turned that trust into a sustained, plain-spoken call to protect biodiversity and cut plastic pollution.
candidates.objections: He has been criticised for past comments framing human population growth as a driver of environmental harm, which some saw as blaming poorer countries.

candidates.rationale: Diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson's disease in 1991, he went public and in 2000 founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation, which has funded more than two billion dollars of research. His warmth and humour about living with the disease changed how the public sees people with Parkinson's.

After redefining political satire on The Daily Show, he spent years lobbying Congress for sick 9/11 first responders, including searing 2019 testimony that helped make their compensation fund permanent. He then campaigned for the 2022 PACT Act, which expanded care for veterans exposed to toxic burn pits.

After Côte d'Ivoire qualified for the 2006 World Cup, he led his teammates in a televised plea on their knees for the warring sides to lay down arms, and later helped bring a national team match to the rebel-held city of Bouaké. His foundation has supported health and education projects in the country, including a hospital in Abidjan.
candidates.objections: His foundation drew a 2016 UK Charity Commission inquiry after press reports questioned how donated funds had been spent.

candidates.rationale: His travel guides and public-television series taught generations of Americans to travel with curiosity and respect for other cultures. He donated an apartment complex to house homeless mothers and their children, and taxes his own company's carbon footprint to fund climate-focused charities.

A physician who founded the Gesundheit! Institute in 1971 to model free, compassionate, joyful medical care, he has led volunteer clowning trips to hospitals, orphanages and refugee camps around the world. The 1998 film about his life spread his argument that humour and human connection belong at the heart of medicine.

The first Black man to win Wimbledon was also an outspoken opponent of apartheid who was arrested protesting outside the South African embassy in 1985. After contracting HIV from a blood transfusion, he spent his final year fighting stigma and founded a foundation to defeat AIDS.

He created the Muppets and helped shape Sesame Street, which has taught letters, numbers and kindness to children worldwide since 1969. His characters modelled warmth, inclusion and silliness for generations of families.

His Discworld novels used comedy to skewer prejudice, cruelty and power, and remain loved by millions of readers. After his early-onset Alzheimer's diagnosis he donated a million dollars to research and campaigned openly for dementia funding and the right to die with dignity.

On The Joy of Painting from 1983 to 1994 he taught millions of viewers to paint landscapes in half an hour, insisting there are no mistakes, only happy accidents. His gentleness and encouragement made art feel possible for people who had never picked up a brush.

His black-and-white photographs of labourers, migrants and famine gave dignity and visibility to people often ignored by the world. With his wife Lélia Wanick Salgado he founded Instituto Terra, which replanted millions of trees on degraded land in Brazil's Atlantic Forest.
candidates.objections: Some critics argued his images aestheticised suffering, turning poverty into beautiful pictures for gallery audiences.

candidates.rationale: At a time when few celebrities would say the word AIDS, she co-founded amfAR in 1985 and later her own AIDS foundation. She lobbied governments and raised large sums for research and care when people with HIV were being shunned.

He gave up his title and years of his prime rather than fight in Vietnam, and his conviction was overturned by the Supreme Court in 1971. He later became a global humanitarian figure and a symbol of courage in living with Parkinson's disease.
candidates.objections: In his Nation of Islam years he voiced support for racial separatism, and his cruel taunting of Joe Frazier drew lasting criticism.

candidates.rationale: In 1947 he broke Major League Baseball's colour line, enduring abuse with extraordinary restraint and opening the sport to Black players. He went on to work for civil rights causes and business development in Black communities.
candidates.objections: He testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1949 against Paul Robeson's statements, which he later said he regretted.

candidates.rationale: She won 39 Grand Slam titles, founded the Women's Tennis Association and fought for equal prize money, beating Bobby Riggs in the 1973 Battle of the Sexes. As one of the first prominent openly gay athletes she became a lifelong advocate for LGBTQ and gender equality.

The two-time World Cup winner helped lead the US women's team fight for equal pay, which ended in a 2022 settlement guaranteeing equal compensation. As an openly gay athlete she has been a prominent advocate for LGBTQ rights and racial justice.

In 2016 he began kneeling during the national anthem to protest police brutality and racial injustice, a stand that effectively ended his NFL career. He has funded youth education programmes through his Know Your Rights Camp.
candidates.objections: His protest divided public opinion, with critics calling it disrespectful to the flag and the military.

candidates.rationale: The winner of 11 NBA titles was also the league's first Black head coach and marched with Martin Luther King Jr. He spoke out against racism throughout his career, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011.

After a record-setting NBA career he became a prolific author and essayist writing about race, history and justice. He founded a foundation that brings science and technology education to underserved children.

In 2017 he founded Common Goal, pledging one percent of his salary to football-based charities and inviting other players to do the same. Hundreds of players, coaches and clubs have since joined the pledge.

The calypso star used his wealth and fame to bankroll the civil rights movement, including bail money and funding for the Freedom Rides. He later helped organise We Are the World and campaigned against apartheid.

A celebrated bass-baritone and actor, he used his fame to campaign against lynching, segregation and colonialism. He paid for it with a revoked passport and a blacklisted career during the McCarthy era.
candidates.objections: He defended Stalin's Soviet Union and did not publicly condemn its purges.

candidates.rationale: In 1985 he co-founded Farm Aid, which has held benefit concerts every year since to support struggling family farmers. His music and generosity made him one of America's most beloved figures.
candidates.objections: He had a long public dispute with the IRS over unpaid taxes in the 1990s.

candidates.rationale: She has been a leading voice for LGBTQ rights, including campaigning to repeal Don't Ask, Don't Tell. With her mother she founded the Born This Way Foundation, focused on youth mental health.
candidates.objections: She apologised in 2019 for a 2013 duet with R. Kelly and removed it from streaming.

candidates.rationale: One of the best-selling musicians in history, he founded the Elton John AIDS Foundation in 1992. It has raised hundreds of millions of dollars for HIV prevention, treatment and fighting stigma.
After his death it became clear he had given millions privately, including to Childline, AIDS charities and individuals in need. He also stood as a gay icon who refused to be shamed.
She became the first deaf performer to win an Academy Award in 1987. She has since campaigned for closed captioning and deaf representation in film and television.

His Mi Sangre foundation has supported landmine victims and peace education in Colombia. He organised the Paz Sin Fronteras concerts on the Colombia-Venezuela border and in Havana to promote peace across political divides.

One of Africa's most celebrated singers, he brought mbalax to the world and has used his fame to campaign against malaria and for debt relief. He also founded a media group and served as Senegal's minister of culture.
The Grammy-winning singer is a long-serving UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. She founded the Batonga Foundation to support girls' education in Africa.
Known as Mama Africa, she carried South African music to the world while exiled for 31 years. She testified against apartheid at the United Nations.
He made reggae a global music of liberation and hope. In 1978 at the One Love Peace Concert he brought Jamaica's two rival political leaders onstage to join hands amid political violence.

He carried folk songs like We Shall Overcome into the civil rights movement and defied the House Un-American Activities Committee. He later founded the Clearwater sloop project that helped clean up the Hudson River.
candidates.objections: He belonged to the Communist Party in the 1940s and was slow to criticise Stalin, which he later called a mistake.

candidates.rationale: Her voice was part of the soundtrack of the civil rights and anti-war movements, and she sang at the March on Washington. She has worked for human rights causes for more than six decades.
His 1991 announcement that he had HIV shattered stereotypes and pushed the disease into mainstream conversation. His foundation has supported HIV testing and education.
He won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, puncturing Nazi propaganda about racial supremacy. He returned to a segregated America and became a symbol of dignity under injustice.

After winning the 200 metres at the 1968 Olympics, he raised a black-gloved fist on the podium to protest racial injustice. He was expelled from the Games and faced years of hostility before being honoured.
The 1968 Olympic bronze medallist raised his fist alongside Tommie Smith in protest at racial injustice. He paid for it with death threats and years of hardship, and later worked in youth mentoring.

The Australian silver medallist wore a human rights badge on the 1968 podium in solidarity with Tommie Smith and John Carlos. He was sidelined at home, and received a posthumous apology from the Australian parliament in 2012.

In 1967 she became the first woman to run the Boston Marathon as a registered entrant, even after an official tried to drag her off the course. She campaigned for women's marathon running to become an Olympic event.
The first lifeguard at Oahu's Waimea Bay was credited with saving hundreds of lives. In 1978 he died after paddling off to seek help when the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa capsized.
From 1985 to 1987 he wheeled more than 40,000 km through 34 countries on his Man in Motion World Tour. His foundation has since supported spinal cord research and accessibility.

After a 1995 riding accident left him paralysed, he became a leading advocate for spinal cord injury research and for people living with paralysis. His foundation continues to fund research and support.
One of the most beloved comedians of his era, he co-hosted Comic Relief USA, which raised millions for homeless people. He made repeated USO tours to entertain troops.
As Lieutenant Uhura on Star Trek she was one of the first Black women in a major television role. She later worked with NASA to recruit women and minority astronauts.
The Hong Kong star has pledged to leave most of his fortune to charity. He is known for his frugal lifestyle.
The Bollywood star hosted Satyamev Jayate, which tackled social issues. He co-founded the Paani Foundation, which helps villages in drought-hit Maharashtra conserve water.
During India's 2020 COVID-19 lockdown he organised buses and flights to help stranded migrant workers get home. He later helped arrange oxygen and medical support for people who needed it.
candidates.objections: In 2021 the income tax department accused him of tax evasion, which he denied.

candidates.rationale: In 2009 she led a campaign that won Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army the right to settle in the UK. She has supported many charities.
candidates.objections: She championed the costly London Garden Bridge project, which was abandoned in 2017.

candidates.rationale: At 99 he began walking laps of his garden in April 2020, raising over £32 million for NHS charities. His cheerfulness became a symbol of hope.
candidates.objections: After his death, the Charity Commission found mismanagement at the foundation run by his family.

candidates.rationale: The writer of Four Weddings and a Funeral and Notting Hill co-founded Comic Relief, which has raised over a billion pounds. He helped launch Make Poverty History.
He became the first Black captain of South Africa's rugby team and led it to World Cup wins in 2019 and 2023. His foundation works on food security and gender-based violence.
The Aboriginal sprinter lit the cauldron at the 2000 Sydney Olympics and won the 400 metres. Her foundation supports education in remote Indigenous communities.
The AFL star and Australian of the Year spoke out against racism in football. He faced sustained booing, prompting a reckoning with racism in Australian sport.
The Wiradjuri tennis player won seven Grand Slam singles titles. Her foundation uses tennis to support Indigenous children's education.
The South African comedian hosted The Daily Show and wrote Born a Crime. His foundation supports education in South Africa.
candidates.objections: Old offensive jokes about women and Jewish people were criticised when he took over The Daily Show in 2015.

candidates.rationale: Her YouTube videos teach toddlers language and speech. She has spoken out for children in conflict zones.
candidates.objections: Critics including pro-Israel advocacy groups accused her of one-sidedness in her advocacy for children in Gaza.

candidates.rationale: His shows used food to explore the lives of ordinary people around the world. He championed kitchen workers.
She became the first openly trans person nominated for a Primetime Emmy for acting. She has used her visibility to advocate for trans people.
She overcame childhood polio to win three gold medals at the 1960 Olympics. She insisted her hometown celebration be integrated.
The Oglala Lakota runner won the 10,000 metres at the 1964 Olympics. He co-founded Running Strong for American Indian Youth.
The world-record marathon runner founded the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation, which organises peace races. She led the Refugee Olympic Team.
The seven-time Formula One champion has pushed for diversity in motorsport. He founded Mission 44.

The most decorated gymnast in history testified before the US Senate in 2021 about the FBI's failures in the Larry Nassar abuse case. Her decision to withdraw at the Tokyo Olympics to protect her mental health shifted the conversation around athlete wellbeing.
She campaigned for equal prize money at Wimbledon, which it adopted in 2007. She has won seven Grand Slam singles titles.
The musician led the campaign to make Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday a US federal holiday. He has used his music for anti-apartheid causes.
He was the first Black man to win the Academy Award for Best Actor. His roles brought dignity to Black characters.
Hamilton reimagined American history with a diverse cast. He raised funds for hurricane relief in Puerto Rico.
He co-founded WITNESS in 1992, which trains activists to use video to document human rights abuses. He founded the WOMAD festival.
His street art spread messages about AIDS awareness and safe sex. He founded a foundation to support AIDS organisations.
His films at Studio Ghibli champion nature, peace and resilient heroines. He has spoken out against war.
His 1964 painting The Problem We All Live With depicted Ruby Bridges walking to school. His art celebrated ordinary American life.
Peanuts has delighted readers for decades. In 1968 he introduced Franklin, a Black character.

His 1958 novel Things Fall Apart told the story of colonialism from an African point of view and became one of the most widely read books in modern African literature. As an editor and teacher he opened doors for a generation of African writers.

The first African laureate of the Nobel Prize in Literature was imprisoned for nearly two years during Nigeria's civil war for trying to broker peace. He has spent decades writing and speaking against military dictatorship and abuse of power.

Novels such as Beloved and Song of Solomon gave Black American history and inner life a central place in world literature, and earned her the 1993 Nobel Prize. As an editor at Random House she championed Black writers.
In essays such as The Fire Next Time he confronted American racism with unflinching honesty and moral clarity. His novels portrayed gay and Black lives with a tenderness rare for his era.

Her memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings spoke openly about trauma, racism and resilience, and helped many survivors find their voice. She worked with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X in the civil rights movement.
One Hundred Years of Solitude made Latin American storytelling a global phenomenon and won him the 1982 Nobel Prize. He also founded a foundation to train journalists in Latin America.
candidates.objections: He was criticised for his long friendship with Fidel Castro despite Cuba's repression of dissidents.

candidates.rationale: The first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature captured Cairo's everyday life in the Cairo Trilogy. He survived a 1994 stabbing by extremists and kept defending free expression.
The Nobel laureate's novels explore the meeting of East and West in Istanbul. He was prosecuted in 2005 for speaking publicly about the Armenian genocide and the killing of Kurds.

She built polyphonic books from interviews with ordinary people about war, Chernobyl and the Soviet collapse, and won the 2015 Nobel Prize. She was a member of the opposition's Coordination Council after Belarus's disputed 2020 election.

She kept writing through Stalin's terror, when her son was imprisoned and her work was banned. Her poem cycle Requiem, memorised by friends rather than written down, bore witness to the suffering of millions.
Regarded as the Palestinian national poet, he wrote about exile, memory and love in language read across the Arab world. His work gave voice to displacement and longing for home.
His Apu Trilogy and other films brought the lives of ordinary Bengalis to world cinema with great humanity. He received an honorary Academy Award in 1992.
The Oscar-winning composer campaigned against nuclear power after Fukushima and founded a forest conservation group. He organised benefit concerts for disaster victims.
Her prints and sculptures depicted poverty, hunger and war's toll on mothers and children. The Nazis banned her work, but her anti-war images remain powerful.
As a student she designed the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, which reshaped how nations remember the dead of war. Her What Is Missing? project memorialises vanishing species.
Her story quilts and paintings told the history of Black America and women's struggles. Her children's book Tar Beach is widely loved.
In 1993 he founded Project Row Houses in Houston's Third Ward, turning shotgun houses into art spaces and housing for young mothers. He received a MacArthur Fellowship.
His photographs for Life documented poverty and racism in America, and his image American Gothic became iconic. He was the first Black director of a major Hollywood film.
Her Migrant Mother and other Depression-era photographs brought the plight of displaced farm families to national attention. She also documented the internment of Japanese Americans.
Their portraits document Black LGBTQ lives in South Africa, creating a record of queer people often erased or targeted by violence. Muholi describes the work as visual activism.
The jazz trumpeter wrote Bring Him Back Home, which became an anthem for the release of Nelson Mandela. He spent decades in exile using music to oppose apartheid.
A founder of Tropicália, he was jailed and exiled by Brazil's military dictatorship in 1969. As culture minister from 2003 to 2008 he championed free culture.
The voice of the Nueva Canción movement, she was arrested onstage and forced into exile by Argentina's military junta. She returned to sing for democracy.
His songs championed workers and the poor. He was tortured and killed by the military after the 1973 coup.
In 1975 he founded El Sistema, a free music education programme that has reached hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan children. The model has been copied in dozens of countries.
