candidates.objections: Critics have described El Sistema as authoritarian in culture and close to successive governments.

candidates.rationale: The great cellist sheltered the dissident writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn at his dacha and was stripped of Soviet citizenship. He played Bach at the fallen Berlin Wall in 1989.
He refused to perform in countries that recognised Franco's regime. At the UN in 1971 he played Song of the Birds and spoke for peace.
When she was barred from Constitution Hall in 1939, she sang for 75,000 people at the Lincoln Memorial. In 1955 she became the first Black soloist at the Metropolitan Opera.
Her Booker-winning The God of Small Things was followed by decades of essays on dams, displacement and civil liberties. She has been repeatedly prosecuted for her speech.
candidates.objections: Critics accuse her of sympathy for Maoist insurgents.

candidates.rationale: He lived under a death fatwa for years after The Satanic Verses and later championed free expression as PEN president. He survived a 2022 stabbing attack and wrote about it in Knife.
One of Israel's most celebrated writers, he helped found Peace Now in 1978. He argued for a two-state solution for decades.
An Auschwitz survivor, he wrote If This Is a Man and other clear-eyed testimonies. His work shaped how the world remembers the Holocaust.
Her diary, written while hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam, has been read by millions. It remains one of the most powerful testimonies of the Holocaust.
The creator of Pippi Longstocking championed children's rights. Her 1978 peace prize speech against violence toward children helped build support for Sweden's 1979 ban on corporal punishment.
Her Moomin books told gentle stories of acceptance and difference. She also drew satirical cartoons mocking Hitler and Stalin.
Despite a filmmaking ban and imprisonment by Iranian authorities, he kept making films. His It Was Just an Accident won the Palme d'Or in 2025.
The Crimean filmmaker was imprisoned by Russia and went on a 145-day hunger strike. He was released in 2019 and later joined the Ukrainian army.
A founding member of Pussy Riot, she served nearly two years in prison for a protest performance in Moscow's cathedral. She has since campaigned for prisoners' rights.
The novelist turned to documenting Russian war crimes after 2022. She died in 2023 after being wounded in a missile strike on a restaurant in Kramatorsk.
He founded the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater in 1958, bringing Black cultural experience to modern dance. His Revelations is one of the most-performed modern dances.
He built a primary school in his home village of Gando with local labour and materials. In 2022 he became the first African winner of the Pritzker Prize.
He designs emergency shelters from paper tubes and other low-cost materials for disaster survivors. He won the 2014 Pritzker Prize.
The British-born architect settled in India and built low-cost homes and buildings in Kerala from local materials. His approach influenced sustainable architecture.
The Palmyra antiquities chief spent decades protecting the site. In 2015 ISIS killed him after he reportedly refused to reveal where artefacts had been hidden.
While working at the Jeu de Paume during the Nazi occupation, she secretly recorded the looting of artworks. Her records helped return tens of thousands of works.
His graphic novel Maus told his father's story of surviving Auschwitz and won a Pulitzer Prize. It showed that comics could carry history.
The Abenaki filmmaker has made dozens of documentaries on Indigenous lives and struggles, including Kanehsatake: 270 Years of Resistance. Her films are a record of First Nations history.
His song Took the Children Away told of the Stolen Generations, of whom he was one. He became a voice for Aboriginal Australians.
His anti-war songs spoke of the suffering of the Vietnam War. They were loved across the country.
Her novels exposed life under apartheid, and several were banned. She won the 1991 Nobel Prize.
His plays such as Master Harold... and the Boys confronted apartheid with humanity. He worked with Black actors at a time when it was dangerous.
The Wassoulou singer has used her music to criticise polygamy and child marriage. She is a powerful voice for women in Mali.
Often called the father of African cinema, he made films about colonialism and African life. His Moolaadé attacked female genital mutilation.
His book Open Veins of Latin America became a classic history of exploitation. He was exiled by the dictatorships of Uruguay and Argentina.
Her science fiction and fantasy imagined gender, power and utopia in fresh ways. She defended writers' rights.
Her books spoke honestly to young readers about growing up. She has fought censorship of books.
The Nobel laureate wrote about Northern Ireland's Troubles with nuance. His poems remain widely loved.
The Muscogee poet was the first Native American US Poet Laureate. She has championed Native poetry.

Founded the Equal Justice Initiative in Alabama in 1989 and has won relief for well over a hundred people on death row. He also created the National Memorial for Peace and Justice, which honours the victims of lynching by name.

He was the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington and taught nonviolent strategy to the young civil rights movement. He did so while being an openly gay man at a time when that cost him dearly, and was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

Her 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat in Montgomery sparked the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott. A long-time NAACP investigator of sexual violence against Black women, she kept working for justice in Detroit for decades afterwards.

Her meticulous investigative reporting in the 1890s exposed lynching as racial terror rather than justice, at great personal risk. She co-founded the NAACP and received a posthumous Pulitzer Prize special citation in 2020.

After escaping slavery in 1838 he became the most powerful abolitionist voice of his era, publishing his own narrative and the newspaper The North Star. He also championed women's suffrage at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention.
As chief counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund he argued and won Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. He became the first Black justice of the US Supreme Court, serving from 1967 to 1991.
She led the Nashville lunch-counter sit-ins and insisted the 1961 Freedom Rides continue after riders were attacked. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2022.

Nine months before Rosa Parks, 15-year-old Colvin was arrested in Montgomery for refusing to give up her bus seat. She was a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle, the case that ended bus segregation in Alabama.

A World War II veteran, he investigated racist violence and organised voter registration and boycotts as the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi. He was assassinated outside his home in 1963.

After escaping slavery she became the first Black woman to win a US court case against a white man, recovering her enslaved son. Her speeches, including the one remembered as 'Ain't I a Woman?', linked abolition and women's rights.

Their legal writing on sex and race discrimination shaped arguments later used by Thurgood Marshall and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and they co-founded the National Organization for Women. They became the first Black woman ordained an Episcopal priest in 1977.

Taxed as a stranger after the death of her wife, she sued the federal government and won United States v. Windsor in 2013, striking down a core part of the Defense of Marriage Act. The ruling paved the way for national marriage equality.

She led the 1977 Section 504 sit-in in San Francisco, occupying a federal building for nearly a month until disability rights regulations were signed. She later helped shape the Americans with Disabilities Act and served as a US special advisor on international disability rights.

Paralysed by polio, he fought his way into the University of California, Berkeley and helped found the Center for Independent Living. He is widely regarded as the father of the independent living movement for disabled people.

An Ojibwe economist and activist, she co-founded Honor the Earth and has worked for decades to restore tribal land and food sovereignty. She has been a leading voice against oil pipelines crossing treaty lands.

He refused to go to a Japanese American incarceration camp in 1942 and challenged the order to the Supreme Court. His conviction was vacated in 1983 and he spent his later life speaking against civil liberties abuses.
An investigative journalist, she exposed forced labour on South African farms and was detained without trial. She was killed by a parcel bomb sent by the apartheid security police in Maputo in 1982.

He co-founded the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee in 1897, the first organisation to campaign for gay rights, and later the Institute for Sexual Science in Berlin. The Nazis looted and burned its library in 1933.

When her 14-year-old son Emmett was murdered in Mississippi in 1955, she insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what racism had done. The photographs galvanised the civil rights movement, and she spent her life teaching.
A refugee who became a garment tycoon, he founded Apple Daily, Hong Kong's most outspoken pro-democracy newspaper. He chose to stay and has been imprisoned since 2020 under the national security law.
candidates.objections: His tabloid publications were criticised for sensationalism.

candidates.rationale: She documented abductions, torture and killings in Chechnya for the human rights group Memorial. She was abducted and murdered in 2009.

As editor of the bilingual weekly Agos, he pushed for Turkish-Armenian reconciliation and open discussion of the Armenian genocide. He was assassinated outside his office in 2007, and 100,000 people marched at his funeral.
She co-founded the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan and defended bonded labourers, religious minorities and women in court. She also served as a UN special rapporteur.
She founded Freedom and Roam Uganda and challenged Ugandan tabloids that outed LGBTQ people, at great personal risk. She won the Martin Ennals Award for Human Rights Defenders in 2011.
He led the campaign that won demarcation of the Yanomami territory in 1992, protecting it from illegal miners. He received the Right Livelihood Award in 2019.
She has led the search for children stolen from disappeared parents during Argentina's dictatorship, helping identify well over 100 of them. In 2014 she found her own grandson.
His decade-long case led to the 1992 Mabo decision, overturning the doctrine of terra nullius in Australia. It recognised native title for Indigenous Australians.

In 1966 he led the Wave Hill walk-off, a strike by Aboriginal stockmen against poor pay and conditions. It sparked the land rights movement and ended with Gough Whitlam pouring sand into his hand in 1975.
He published The Liberator for 35 years, demanding immediate emancipation. He co-founded the American Anti-Slavery Society and also supported women's rights.
He kept publishing antislavery editorials though mobs destroyed his presses repeatedly. He was killed defending his press in Alton, Illinois in 1837, and is remembered as a martyr to press freedom.
His 1789 autobiography described being kidnapped and enslaved as a child. It became a bestseller that fuelled the British abolition movement.
He travelled tens of thousands of miles gathering evidence of the slave trade's horrors, which he published. His research underpinned Britain's 1807 abolition of the slave trade.
Her 1792 book A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women deserve education equal to men. She is considered a founder of feminist philosophy.

After learning her husband had drugged her and invited dozens of men to rape her, she waived her anonymity for the 2024 trial. Her declaration that shame must change sides became a global rallying call.
As Hesse's attorney general he organised the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials. He also passed crucial information on Adolf Eichmann's location to Israel.

Her 1991 Senate testimony that Clarence Thomas had sexually harassed her brought workplace harassment into national debate and was followed by a surge in harassment complaints. She has since spent decades as a law professor and chair of a Hollywood commission working to end harassment.

She began using the phrase 'Me Too' in 2006 to build solidarity among survivors of sexual violence, especially young Black women and girls. When the phrase went viral in 2017, she kept the focus on healing and support for survivors.

The law professor coined the term 'intersectionality' in 1989 to describe how race and sex discrimination compound for Black women, a framework now used worldwide. She co-founded the African American Policy Forum and its #SayHerName campaign remembering Black women killed by police.

The Australian comedian and journalist edited the ABC's disability website Ramp Up and coined the phrase 'inspiration porn' for the way disabled people are held up to make others feel good. Her widely viewed 2014 TED talk argued for being treated as ordinary rather than inspirational.

Her memoir Redefining Realness, about growing up trans and Native Hawaiian, became a New York Times bestseller. As a writer, director and producer on the series Pose she helped put trans women of colour at the centre of mainstream television.

Taiwan's most famous gay rights campaigner came out publicly in 1986 and kept petitioning for marriage equality for three decades. His petition led to the 2017 Constitutional Court ruling that made Taiwan the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2019.

A veteran Afghan women's rights advocate, she chose to stay in Kabul after the Taliban took power in 2021. She has continued to run a shelter for women and to speak publicly against the restrictions on Afghan women and girls.

She fasted for 16 years, from 2000 to 2016, in protest against the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act in Manipur after a massacre of civilians. Force-fed through a nasal tube for most of that time, she became a symbol of nonviolent resistance.

The journalist and activist co-founded Citizens for Justice and Peace to pursue legal cases on behalf of victims of the 2002 Gujarat riots. Her work helped secure convictions in several massacre cases, and she has faced repeated prosecutions in return.

She founded the Humanitarian Law Center in Belgrade in 1992 to document war crimes committed during the Yugoslav wars, regardless of who committed them. Its records supported prosecutions at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

The Saudi blogger created a website for open debate about religion and politics and was sentenced to ten years in prison and 1,000 lashes. His case became a worldwide symbol of free expression, and he won the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize in 2015.

The first Indigenous judge in Manitoba, he chaired Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission into the residential school system. Its 2015 report documented the abuse of Indigenous children and issued 94 calls to action.

The Ponca chief was arrested in 1879 after leaving Indian Territory to bury his son in his homeland. His lawsuit produced a landmark ruling that a Native American is a person under US law with the right to habeas corpus.

His rooftop radio reports from London during the Blitz brought the war home to Americans. In 1954 his See It Now broadcast on Senator Joseph McCarthy helped turn the public against the anti-communist witch hunts.
As anchor of the CBS Evening News for 19 years he was often called 'the most trusted man in America'. His 1968 on-air assessment that the Vietnam War was a stalemate shifted national opinion.

She had herself committed to the women's asylum on Blackwell's Island in 1887 and exposed its cruelty in Ten Days in a Mad-House, prompting reforms. She also travelled around the world in a record 72 days.
Her meticulously documented History of the Standard Oil Company exposed the monopoly's practices. It helped lead to the Supreme Court's 1911 break-up of Standard Oil.
A chemical technician and union activist at a plutonium plant in Oklahoma, she documented safety violations. She died in a 1974 car crash on her way to meet a New York Times reporter.
The former research chief at Brown & Williamson revealed that tobacco executives knew nicotine was addictive and manipulated its effect. His testimony supported the 1998 tobacco settlement.

With Bob Woodward at The Washington Post he uncovered the Watergate scandal, which led to President Nixon's resignation in 1974. Their book All the President's Men became a model for investigative reporting.
His Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein won The Washington Post a Pulitzer Prize and led to Nixon's resignation. He has written more than 20 books on American presidencies.
candidates.objections: He has been criticised for access journalism and for holding back newsworthy material for his books.

candidates.rationale: As publisher of The Washington Post she backed publishing the Pentagon Papers and the Watergate investigation despite heavy government pressure. Her memoir Personal History won the 1998 Pulitzer Prize.
She moderated two vice-presidential debates and co-anchored PBS NewsHour, the first Black woman to co-anchor a national evening news broadcast. She was admired for fair, rigorous questioning.
She reported from the siege of Sarajevo and the Rwandan genocide, refusing false balance between aggressors and victims. She has been CNN's chief international anchor for years.
She reported from war zones for The Sunday Times, losing an eye in Sri Lanka in 2001. She was killed by Syrian government shelling in Homs in 2012, after reporting on civilian suffering there.
Her blog Running Commentary exposed corruption among Malta's political and business elite. She was killed by a car bomb in 2017, and the outcry led to the resignation of the prime minister.

He investigated tax fraud and links between businessmen and politicians in Slovakia. He and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová were murdered in 2018, sparking mass protests that brought down the government.
The editor of the Kannada weekly Lankesh Patrike wrote against communal violence and caste discrimination. She was shot dead outside her home in Bengaluru in 2017.

For 25 years she reported from the West Bank and Gaza for Al Jazeera, becoming one of the Arab world's most recognised journalists. She was shot dead while covering a raid in Jenin in 2022, wearing a vest marked 'Press'.

The Wall Street Journal's South Asia bureau chief was kidnapped and murdered in Pakistan in 2002. His family created the Daniel Pearl Foundation to promote cross-cultural understanding through journalism and music.
He reported from conflicts in Libya and Syria. He was kidnapped in Syria in 2012 and murdered by the Islamic State in 2014, and his family founded a foundation for hostage recovery.
A Wall Street Journal reporter in Moscow, he was arrested in 2023 on espionage charges that he, his newspaper and the US government rejected. He was freed in the August 2024 prisoner swap.
She wrote about the legacy of the Troubles and her experience as a young gay woman in Belfast. She was shot dead while observing rioting in Derry in 2019.
She exposed Dublin's drug lords in the Sunday Independent despite being shot and assaulted. Her murder in 1996 led to the creation of Ireland's Criminal Assets Bureau.
He co-founded the weekly Ríodoce in Sinaloa and wrote books about the victims of the drug war. He was murdered in 2017.
Her 2005 book exposed a child sexual abuse ring involving powerful businessmen. She was arrested and abused in custody, and later won a UN Human Rights Committee ruling against Mexico.

Posing as an American filmmaker, she secretly recorded senior Gujarat officials about the 2002 riots and extrajudicial killings, publishing the transcripts as Gujarat Files. She has kept reporting despite sustained online abuse and legal pressure.
candidates.objections: Indian authorities have pursued money-laundering charges over her crowdfunding for pandemic relief, which she denies and press-freedom groups describe as harassment.

candidates.rationale: His book Everybody Loves a Good Drought and years of reporting as rural affairs editor of The Hindu documented poverty and farmer suicides in India's countryside. He founded the People's Archive of Rural India to record the lives of rural people, and won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2007.
The Novaya Gazeta reporter broke the 2017 story of the detention and torture of gay men in Chechnya. She kept reporting on the region despite threats and was badly beaten there in 2023.

As editor-in-chief of Cumhuriyet he published footage in 2015 of Turkish intelligence trucks carrying weapons to Syria. He was sentenced to prison, survived a gunman's attack outside the courthouse, and continues his journalism from exile.

The Shargh reporter was among the first to report on Mahsa Amini's hospitalisation in 2022, the story that sparked the Woman, Life, Freedom protests. She was imprisoned for her reporting and, with Elaheh Mohammadi, received the 2023 UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize.

The Radio Free Europe reporter exposed hidden business holdings of Azerbaijan's ruling family. She was jailed from 2014 to 2016 on charges widely seen as retaliation and won the UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize.

The Associated Press video journalist was among the last international reporters inside besieged Mariupol in 2022, documenting the bombing of a maternity hospital. His film 20 Days in Mariupol won the 2024 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, Ukraine's first Oscar.

The Chicago broadcaster recorded the voices of ordinary Americans in oral histories such as Working and The Good War, which won the Pulitzer Prize. His archive of thousands of interviews is a lasting record of everyday life in the twentieth century.

His 2017 New Yorker reporting documented sexual assault allegations against Harvey Weinstein despite intense pressure to kill the story. It shared the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service and helped ignite the Me Too reckoning.

With Megan Twohey she broke the October 2017 New York Times investigation into Harvey Weinstein, persuading women to go on the record. The reporting shared the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service and is told in their book She Said.

With Jodi Kantor she reported the 2017 New York Times investigation into Harvey Weinstein that helped launch the global Me Too movement. She had earlier exposed an underground network for 'rehoming' adopted children in the US.

Her 2018 Miami Herald series Perversion of Justice revealed how Jeffrey Epstein's victims had been failed by a lenient plea deal. It led to his 2019 arrest and the resignation of Labor Secretary Alex Acosta.

His documentaries, including The Civil War, Jazz and The Vietnam War, have brought careful, source-rich American history to tens of millions of viewers. He has made public television a home for long-form historical truth-telling.

Her documentary 13th traced the line from slavery to mass incarceration, and her series When They See Us told the story of the Exonerated Five. She also directed Selma and founded ARRAY to distribute films by women and people of colour.
His 1988 documentary The Thin Blue Line uncovered evidence that helped free Randall Dale Adams, wrongly convicted of murder in Texas. He later won an Academy Award for The Fog of War.

His documentaries Ethnic Notions and Tongues Untied examined anti-Black stereotypes and gave Black gay men a voice on public television. He kept making films until his death from AIDS-related illness in 1994.

His 1947 book From Slavery to Freedom established African American history as a serious field and remains in print. He assisted the NAACP legal team in Brown v. Board of Education and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1995.

The historian was sued for libel by Holocaust denier David Irving and won in 2000, with the court finding that Irving had distorted history. She later served as the US Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism.
Her 1997 bestseller The Rape of Nanking brought the 1937 massacre of Chinese civilians to wide Western attention. She also wrote histories of Chinese Americans before her death in 2004.
candidates.objections: Some historians criticised factual errors and a lack of nuance in The Rape of Nanking.

candidates.rationale: A former Facebook product manager, she disclosed tens of thousands of internal documents in 2021 showing the company knew about harms such as Instagram's effect on teenage girls. Her Senate testimony fuelled new online-safety laws around the world.

A GCHQ translator, she leaked a 2003 NSA memo asking British help to spy on UN Security Council members before the Iraq war vote. She was charged under the Official Secrets Act, and the case was dropped in 2004.

A Moscow tax adviser, he uncovered a 230-million-dollar tax fraud by Russian officials and testified against them. He was arrested and died in pre-trial detention in 2009 after being denied medical care, inspiring Magnitsky sanctions laws in many countries.

The paediatrician's 2015 research showed rising lead levels in Flint children after the city switched water sources, forcing officials to admit the crisis. Her book What the Eyes Don't See tells the story.

The Vietnam veteran wrote letters to Congress and the Pentagon in 1969 describing the My Lai massacre, which prompted the official investigation. He later became an investigative journalist, and the Ridenhour Prizes for truth-telling are named after him.

He founded Bellingcat in 2014, pioneering open-source investigation with public videos, photos and satellite imagery. Its work helped trace the missile launcher that downed flight MH17 and identify the suspects in the Skripal poisoning.

In 1933 the Welsh journalist walked through Soviet Ukrainian villages and reported the famine now known as the Holodomor, while other correspondents denied it. He was murdered in 1935 while reporting in Inner Mongolia.

As editor of South Africa's Daily Dispatch, he befriended Steve Biko and exposed the truth about Biko's death in police custody. Banned by the apartheid regime, he fled in 1978 and his book Biko became the film Cry Freedom.

A former lawyer, she travelled to Wuhan in early 2020 and posted videos of crowded hospitals and detentions. She was sentenced to four years for 'picking quarrels and provoking trouble' and went on hunger strike in protest.

The publisher of the Argentine newspaper La Opinión reported on the junta's disappearances and was arrested and tortured in 1977. His memoir Prisoner Without a Name, Cell Without a Number exposed the dictatorship's crimes to the world.

The editor of Colombia's El Espectador denounced drug cartels and their corruption of public life. He was murdered on Pablo Escobar's orders in 1986, and UNESCO's World Press Freedom Prize bears his name.

For his 1985 book Ganz unten he spent two years undercover as a Turkish labourer, exposing the exploitation of migrant workers in West Germany. His undercover methods have exposed abuses in many industries.

Her Observer reporting with whistleblower Christopher Wylie exposed Cambridge Analytica's harvesting of Facebook data in 2018. It made her a Pulitzer Prize finalist and prompted inquiries on several continents.
candidates.objections: She lost part of a libel case brought by Brexit donor Arron Banks on appeal in 2023.

candidates.rationale: The Chicago Defender's Washington correspondent pressed Presidents Eisenhower and Kennedy on segregation at White House briefings. Known as the 'First Lady of the Black Press', she became the first Black woman commentator on a US national network.
As Jet and Ebony's Washington bureau chief he covered the Emmett Till murder trial and the Freedom Rides. Jet's publication of Till's open-casket photographs helped awaken a national conscience.

The historian organised Oyneg Shabbos, a secret archive documenting daily life and death in the Warsaw Ghetto, buried in metal boxes and milk cans. Much of it was recovered after the war; he was murdered by the Nazis in 1944.

Salk developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, announced safe and effective in 1955 after a massive field trial. Asked who owned the patent, he famously answered "the people," and the vaccine helped drive polio toward eradication.
Sabin developed the oral polio vaccine, cheap and easy to give by mouth, which became the workhorse of global eradication campaigns. He declined to patent it so it could reach children everywhere.

Jenner showed in 1796 that inoculation with cowpox protected against smallpox, founding the practice of vaccination. His work began the long road to smallpox's eradication in 1980, one of humanity's greatest achievements.
candidates.objections: His 1796 experiment on a young boy, James Phipps, would not meet modern standards of informed consent.

candidates.rationale: Banting co-discovered insulin in 1921-22, turning type 1 diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition. He and his colleagues sold the patent to the University of Toronto for a nominal sum so it could be widely produced.

Karikó spent decades pursuing modified mRNA despite demotions and rejected grants, and with Drew Weissman found the nucleoside modification that made mRNA vaccines possible. Her persistence underpinned COVID-19 vaccines given to billions, earning the 2023 Nobel Prize.

Weissman partnered with Katalin Karikó to show that modified nucleosides let mRNA slip past the immune system's alarms, the key to mRNA vaccines. He has since worked on making vaccines accessible in lower-income countries, including a partnership in Thailand.

Tu led the team that isolated artemisinin in the 1970s, drawing on a fourth-century herbal text, and tested it on herself for safety. Artemisinin-based therapies have saved millions of lives from malaria, and she became China's first woman Nobel laureate in science.

Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 and insisted that CERN release it royalty-free, making it an open commons. He continues to campaign for an open web and for people's control over their own data.

Grandin redesigned livestock handling systems to reduce animal fear and suffering, and much of the North American cattle industry now uses her designs or audit standards. As one of the first people to describe autism from the inside, she has helped change public understanding of neurodiversity.
candidates.objections: Some animal-rights advocates argue that improving slaughter conditions legitimises industrial meat production.

candidates.rationale: Sagan brought the wonder of the cosmos to hundreds of millions through Cosmos and books like Pale Blue Dot, and pushed for the Voyager image of Earth as a 'pale blue dot'. He co-authored the nuclear winter research and warned early and publicly about climate change.

Turing laid the foundations of computer science and led codebreaking work at Bletchley Park that shortened the Second World War. Prosecuted in 1952 for being gay and subjected to chemical castration, he later became a symbol for the pardons of men convicted under anti-gay laws.

Ruit refined a small-incision cataract technique and made intraocular lenses affordable, restoring sight to well over 100,000 people himself. The Tilganga Institute he co-founded trains surgeons across Asia and Africa and manufactures lenses cheaply.

Starting as a teenager in 1979, Payeng planted trees on a barren sandbar of the Brahmaputra for decades, growing the Molai forest now covering hundreds of hectares. The forest shelters elephants, tigers, rhinos and deer, and he became known as the Forest Man of India.
Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, opening the antibiotic era that has saved countless lives. In his Nobel lecture he warned presciently about antibiotic resistance from misuse.
Pasteur's work established germ theory, pasteurisation and vaccines for rabies and anthrax. Pasteurisation alone has prevented enormous numbers of deaths from contaminated milk and food.
candidates.objections: Historians have found his private notebooks show he overstated the testing behind his rabies and anthrax work.

candidates.rationale: Semmelweis showed in 1847 that handwashing with chlorinated lime slashed deaths from childbed fever in a Vienna maternity clinic. Ridiculed in his lifetime, he is now honoured as a pioneer of antiseptic practice.

Snow mapped the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak in London and traced it to a contaminated water pump, arguing against the prevailing 'bad air' theory. His work founded modern epidemiology and helped make the case for clean water.

Hilleman developed more than 40 vaccines, including those for measles, mumps, hepatitis B and Hib, several still on standard childhood schedules. His vaccines are credited with saving millions of lives each year.

Apgar devised the Apgar score in 1952, a quick check of newborns that is still used in delivery rooms worldwide. She later led the March of Dimes' work on preventing birth defects, including promoting rubella vaccination.

Hodgkin determined the structures of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin, earning the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She was a long-time president of the Pugwash Conferences working for nuclear disarmament and helped build crystallography in developing countries.

Franklin's X-ray diffraction work, including Photo 51, was crucial to understanding the double-helix structure of DNA. She also made important advances on the structure of viruses such as tobacco mosaic virus and polio.

As an FDA reviewer in 1960, Kelsey refused to approve thalidomide despite heavy company pressure, sparing the United States the wave of birth defects seen elsewhere. Her stand led to stronger drug-testing laws in 1962.

Hotez co-led development of Corbevax, a low-cost COVID-19 vaccine shared without patent restrictions and given to tens of millions of people in India and Indonesia. He has spent his career on vaccines for neglected diseases of poverty.

Bottazzi co-led the Texas Children's Hospital team behind Corbevax, a patent-free COVID-19 vaccine designed to be cheap to make in lower-income countries. She was nominated with Peter Hotez for the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize.

Kang's decades of research on enteric infections in Indian children were central to developing and testing Rotavac, a low-cost rotavirus vaccine. She was the first Indian woman elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.
Muyembe was among the first scientists to investigate Ebola in 1976 and spent decades fighting outbreaks in the Congo. His work led to mAb114, one of the first effective Ebola treatments.

Henderson directed the WHO's global smallpox eradication campaign from 1966 to 1977, using surveillance and ring vaccination. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, the only human disease wiped out so far.
Maalin was the last person to catch smallpox naturally, in 1977. He spent his later years as a polio vaccination campaigner in Somalia, and died of malaria in 2013 while working on a polio outbreak.

Lovelace wrote what is widely regarded as the first published algorithm for a machine, for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. She foresaw that computers could go beyond numbers to music and symbols.
Hopper built one of the first compilers and championed machine-independent, English-like programming languages that led to COBOL. She spent decades teaching and making computing accessible.

Johnson calculated trajectories for America's first human spaceflights and John Glenn's orbital mission, working through segregation at NASA's Langley centre. Her story, told in Hidden Figures, inspired a generation.

Jemison became the first African American woman in space in 1992, after working as a Peace Corps doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia. She has since championed science education for underrepresented students.
Einstein's theories of relativity and light quanta reshaped physics. He used his fame to fight racism in America, calling it 'a disease of white people', and campaigned for nuclear disarmament.
candidates.objections: His private travel diaries contain disparaging remarks about Chinese people, and his treatment of his first wife was cold.

candidates.rationale: Cousteau co-developed the Aqua-Lung and brought the undersea world to television audiences everywhere. He campaigned successfully against dumping nuclear waste at sea and for protecting Antarctica from mining.
candidates.objections: His early films, including The Silent World, show practices such as dynamiting reefs that harmed marine life.

candidates.rationale: Earle has led more than 100 ocean expeditions and was the first woman to serve as chief scientist of NOAA. Through Mission Blue she has championed 'Hope Spots', marine protected areas around the world.

As a graduate student Bell Burnell discovered the first radio pulsars in 1967, work for which her supervisor, not she, shared the Nobel Prize. She gave the whole of her 2018 Breakthrough Prize, about £2.3 million, to fund physics PhD places for students from underrepresented groups.

Salam shared the 1979 Nobel Prize for electroweak unification, the first Pakistani and first Muslim science laureate. He founded the International Centre for Theoretical Physics in Trieste to support scientists from developing countries.

Bath invented the Laserphaco probe for cataract removal, becoming the first African American woman doctor to receive a medical patent. She co-founded the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness and pioneered community ophthalmology in underserved areas.

Drew developed methods for processing and storing blood plasma and led the Blood for Britain programme in the Second World War. He resigned from the American Red Cross over its racial segregation of blood.

Blackwell was the first woman to earn a medical degree in the United States, in 1849. She co-founded the New York Infirmary for Women and Children and a women's medical college, opening medicine to women.

Shetty founded Narayana Health, which performs heart surgery at a fraction of Western costs through high-volume, efficient care. He also helped create Yeshasvini, a micro-insurance scheme covering millions of farmers.

Venkataswamy founded Aravind Eye Hospital in 1976 after retiring, with a model where paying patients subsidise free care for the poor. Aravind has become one of the world's largest eye care providers, performing millions of surgeries.

Rosling investigated a paralytic disease, konzo, in Mozambique and later co-founded Gapminder to fight misconceptions about global development with data. His talks and the book Factfulness showed millions how much the world has improved.
Nott has volunteered as a surgeon in war zones including Syria, Gaza and Afghanistan for decades. His foundation trains local doctors in trauma surgery for conflict and disaster settings.
Hodes has worked in Ethiopia since the 1980s, arranging life-saving surgery for children with spinal deformities, heart disease and cancer. He has taken many of his patients into his own home.

Corbett was a scientific lead on the NIH Vaccine Research Center team whose coronavirus spike-protein research underpinned the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine. She also made a point of explaining the vaccines to Black communities with well-founded reasons for medical distrust.
Gilbert co-led development of the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, supplied on a not-for-profit basis during the pandemic. More than 2.5 billion doses reached people in over 170 countries.
Şahin co-founded BioNTech with Özlem Türeci and led the rapid development of the first authorised mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. The couple have pursued mRNA cancer immunotherapies for decades.
Türeci co-founded BioNTech and served as chief medical officer as it developed the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. Her research focuses on individualised cancer immunotherapy.
Garrett Anderson was the first woman to qualify as a physician and surgeon in Britain. She founded a hospital staffed by women and later became England's first woman mayor.
Cavell nursed soldiers from all sides in occupied Belgium and helped some 200 Allied soldiers escape. She was executed by a German firing squad in 1915, saying 'patriotism is not enough'.

Taussig, a founder of paediatric cardiology who was herself partly deaf, conceived the Blalock-Taussig shunt that from 1944 saved thousands of 'blue babies' born with heart defects. She also travelled to Europe in 1962 and helped alert the United States to the dangers of thalidomide.

Thomas, without a college degree and paid as a janitor, developed the surgical technique for the Blalock-Taussig shunt. He trained generations of surgeons at Johns Hopkins, which later awarded him an honorary doctorate.

Lown developed the direct-current defibrillator used to restart hearts around the world. He co-founded International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War with Soviet cardiologist Yevgeniy Chazov, and the group won the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize.

Edwards and his students ran independent tests of Flint's tap water in 2015 and exposed dangerous lead levels, work he largely funded himself. He had earlier exposed Washington, D.C.'s lead-in-water crisis of the early 2000s, when official agencies played it down.

Patterson used lead isotopes to calculate the age of the Earth at about 4.55 billion years, and in the process discovered that industrial lead from petrol was contaminating the whole planet. He fought the lead industry for years, and his evidence helped bring about the removal of lead from petrol in the United States.

Needleman's 1979 study of children's baby teeth showed that even low-level lead exposure harmed intelligence and behaviour. His research, defended through industry-backed attacks, helped drive the phase-out of lead from petrol and paint.

With Sherwood Rowland, Molina showed in 1974 that CFCs from aerosols and refrigerants destroy the ozone layer. Their warning led to the Montreal Protocol, the most successful environmental treaty so far, and a shared 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Rowland co-discovered with Mario Molina that CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone, and spent years pressing the case publicly despite fierce industry pushback. Their work led to the Montreal Protocol and a shared 1995 Nobel Prize.

Farman and his British Antarctic Survey colleagues reported the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985, using decades of patient ground measurements. The shock of their discovery helped secure the 1987 Montreal Protocol phasing out CFCs.

Solomon led Antarctic expeditions in the 1980s that explained how chemistry on polar stratospheric clouds creates the ozone hole. Decades later her team documented the first clear signs that the ozone layer is healing.

Hansen's 1988 testimony to the US Senate that global warming had begun brought climate change to wide public attention. The NASA scientist went on to decades of research and advocacy for rapid emissions cuts, including support for young people's climate lawsuits.
candidates.objections: His support for nuclear power and civil-disobedience arrests have divided some fellow scientists and environmentalists.

candidates.rationale: Keeling began precise measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in 1958. The resulting Keeling Curve, showing CO2 rising year after year, became the foundational evidence of human-driven greenhouse gas build-up.

In 1856 Foote showed experimentally that carbon dioxide traps the sun's heat and suggested that more of it would warm the planet, years before John Tyndall's better-known work. She was also a signatory of the 1848 Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments on women's rights.

Mann's 1998-99 'hockey stick' reconstruction showed that recent warming is unusual in at least a thousand years, a finding later confirmed by many independent studies. He has defended climate science through years of political attacks and harassment.
candidates.objections: Critics have found his public style combative, and part of his defamation award was later reduced.

candidates.rationale: Manabe built some of the first physical climate models in the 1960s, showing how rising carbon dioxide warms the Earth's surface. His work laid the groundwork for modern climate projections and won a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Ramanathan discovered in 1975 that CFCs are potent greenhouse gases, and later showed how black carbon soot and other short-lived pollutants warm the climate and harm health. He has worked with the Pontifical Academy of Sciences and faith leaders to promote climate solutions.

Huq founded the International Centre for Climate Change and Development in Dhaka and spent decades championing climate adaptation for the world's poorest countries. He was a leading advocate for the loss-and-damage fund agreed at COP27 in 2022, the year before he died.

Rockström led the development of the 'planetary boundaries' framework, identifying the safe operating limits for Earth's life-support systems. As director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research he is a leading voice on climate tipping points.

Otto co-founded World Weather Attribution, which rapidly measures how far climate change made specific heatwaves, floods and droughts worse. Her work has changed how media and courts talk about the causes of extreme weather.
Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring exposed the dangers of indiscriminate pesticide use. It helped launch the modern environmental movement and the US ban on DDT for agriculture.
candidates.objections: Some critics argue DDT restrictions hampered malaria control, though agricultural use rather than disease control was her target.

candidates.rationale: Leopold pushed for the Gila Wilderness, designated in 1924 as the world's first administratively protected wilderness area. His book A Sand County Almanac set out a 'land ethic' that treats people as members of the land community, shaping modern conservation.

As a US senator from Wisconsin, Nelson conceived Earth Day in 1970, when some 20 million Americans took part, helping spur landmark environmental laws. After leaving office he spent years as counselor to The Wilderness Society.

Douglas's 1947 book The Everglades: River of Grass reframed the wetlands as a living river rather than a worthless swamp. She founded Friends of the Everglades in 1969 and fought for the ecosystem until her death at 108.

Suzuki, a geneticist, has hosted CBC's The Nature of Things since 1979, bringing science and ecology to generations of viewers. The David Suzuki Foundation campaigns for biodiversity, clean energy and Indigenous-led conservation.

Bahuguna helped lead the Chipko movement, in which Himalayan villagers embraced trees to stop commercial logging, and walked thousands of kilometres to spread its message. His campaigning helped win a 1980 ban on green felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh.

In 1974 Gaura Devi led the women of Reni village in the Himalayas to block contractors' loggers by standing guard over the forest. Their nonviolent stand became one of the defining moments of the Chipko movement.

Bhatt's village cooperative organised the first Chipko action in 1973, defending local forests from commercial felling. He went on to lead decades of community-run afforestation in the Himalayas and won the Ramon Magsaysay Award.

Patkar founded the Narmada Bachao Andolan to defend the tens of thousands of villagers displaced by dams on the Narmada River, using fasts and nonviolent protest. Her campaign helped push the World Bank to withdraw from the Sardar Sarovar project.
candidates.objections: Critics argue her opposition delayed water projects intended to benefit drought-prone regions of Gujarat.

candidates.rationale: Singh and his organisation Tarun Bharat Sangh helped Rajasthan villages build thousands of johads, traditional rainwater structures, reviving several dry rivers. He received the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015.

Gowda, from the Halakki Vokkaliga community in Karnataka, planted and nurtured tens of thousands of trees over some six decades. Known as the 'encyclopedia of the forest' for her knowledge of plant species, she received the Padma Shri in 2021.

Sawadogo revived and improved zaï, the traditional practice of digging compost-filled planting pits, to restore degraded Sahel land and grow a forest on once-barren ground. He taught the method to farmers across West Africa and won the Right Livelihood Award in 2018.

Rinaudo promoted farmer-managed natural regeneration in Niger from the 1980s, helping farmers regrow trees from living stumps across millions of hectares. He shared the Right Livelihood Award in 2018 and has spread the technique to over two dozen countries.

Silva, a former rubber tapper who worked alongside Chico Mendes, oversaw a steep fall in Amazon deforestation as Brazil's environment minister from 2003 to 2008. She returned to the post in 2023 and deforestation fell sharply again.

Raoni has campaigned for more than half a century to protect the Amazon and Indigenous territories, including a 1989 world tour with Sting that raised support for Kayapo land. He remains a leading voice against dams and deforestation in the Xingu basin.

Stang spent decades in Pará helping poor farmers claim land and practise sustainable farming against illegal loggers and ranchers. She was shot dead in 2005 on the orders of ranchers, and her death led to new protected areas.

Pereira, an expert with Brazil's Indigenous agency, worked to protect the isolated peoples of the Javari Valley and trained Indigenous patrols against illegal fishing and mining. He was murdered alongside journalist Dom Phillips in 2022.

Phillips reported on the Amazon and its defenders for outlets including The Guardian for over a decade. He was murdered with Bruno Pereira in 2022 while researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.
Paulino was one of the 'Guardians of the Forest', Guajajara volunteers who patrol the Arariboia Indigenous territory against illegal logging. He was killed in an ambush by loggers in 2019.

Baldenegro, a Tarahumara farmer, led nonviolent protests that won a court-ordered halt to logging in the Sierra Madre's old-growth forests. He received the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2005 and was murdered in 2017.

Acuña refused to give up her small farm in Cajamarca to the proposed Conga gold mine despite violent evictions and years of legal battles. Peru's Supreme Court ruled in her favour, and she won the Goldman Prize in 2016.

Márquez organised Afro-Colombian women from La Toma in a 2014 march to Bogotá that got illegal gold miners removed from their land, winning the Goldman Prize in 2018. She became Colombia's first Black woman vice president in 2022.

Suruí, of the Paiter Suruí people, was the only Brazilian Indigenous speaker at the opening of COP26 in 2021. She coordinates the Indigenous youth movement of Rondônia and works with the Kanindé association monitoring deforestation.

Peltier began campaigning as a child for clean drinking water on First Nations reserves and addressed the UN General Assembly in 2018. She was named chief water commissioner of the Anishinabek Nation in 2019.

Martinez has spoken at the UN on climate since he was a teenager and was one of the youth plaintiffs in climate lawsuits against governments. As youth director of Earth Guardians he helped build a global network of young activists.

Ma founded the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, whose public database and maps of factory pollution records pushed thousands of companies to clean up. His book China's Water Crisis was an early warning about the country's rivers.

Miyawaki developed a method of planting dense, native-species mini-forests that grow quickly and support rich biodiversity. His method has been used to plant tens of millions of trees across the world.
Fukuoka developed 'natural farming', growing rice and grains without tilling, chemicals or weeding. His book The One-Straw Revolution inspired permaculture and organic movements worldwide.

Hosokawa, a company doctor at the Chisso factory, showed in experiments on cats that the plant's waste water caused Minamata disease. His deathbed testimony helped win the landmark 1973 court case for victims.

Smith spent three years in Minamata with Aileen Mioko Smith documenting the victims of Chisso's mercury poisoning, and was badly beaten by company employees. His photographs brought the disaster to world attention.

Ibrahim, a Mbororo pastoralist, founded an association for Indigenous women and peoples in Chad and uses participatory mapping to help communities share scarce resources. She has been a prominent voice for Indigenous knowledge in UN climate talks.
Galdikas has studied and protected wild orangutans in Borneo since 1971. Her Orangutan Foundation International runs rescue, rehabilitation and forest protection work.

Schaller has carried out pioneering field studies of gorillas, tigers, lions, giant pandas and snow leopards. His work helped create protected areas across Asia, including the Chang Tang reserve in Tibet.
Kahumbu leads WildlifeDirect and ran the Hands Off Our Elephants campaign, which helped Kenya adopt tougher anti-poaching laws. She makes nature films to connect Kenyans with their wildlife.

Kalema-Zikusoka was Uganda's first wildlife veterinarian and founded Conservation Through Public Health, which improves community health around Bwindi to protect mountain gorillas. She was named a UN Champion of the Earth in 2021.
Anthony travelled to Baghdad during the 2003 invasion and helped keep the surviving animals of the Baghdad Zoo alive. His book The Elephant Whisperer described his work at the Thula Thula reserve.
Brower led the Sierra Club in the 1950s and 1960s and fought dams in Dinosaur National Monument and the Grand Canyon. He founded Friends of the Earth and Earth Island Institute.
Berry has farmed in Kentucky for decades while writing poems, novels and essays such as The Unsettling of America on land, community and farming. He is a leading voice for sustainable agriculture.

Kimmerer, a Potawatomi botanist, wrote Braiding Sweetgrass, which weaves Indigenous knowledge together with plant science and became a long-running bestseller. She founded the Center for Native Peoples and the Environment at SUNY and received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2022.
Richards, the first woman admitted to MIT, led a landmark survey of Massachusetts water that produced the first state water-quality standards. She pioneered environmental health.

Bullard's research from the late 1970s documented that landfills and toxic facilities were disproportionately sited in Black communities. His book Dumping in Dixie and decades of scholarship helped found the environmental justice movement.

After losing her husband to lung cancer, Johnson founded People for Community Recovery in 1979 to fight the toxic pollution surrounding the Altgeld Gardens public housing estate on Chicago's South Side. Her decades of organising earned her the title 'mother of the environmental justice movement'.

Shepard co-founded WE ACT for Environmental Justice in Harlem in 1988 after residents fought a sewage treatment plant sited in their neighbourhood. The group has become a leading voice for clean air and fair environmental policy for communities of colour in New York and nationally.

Gibbs organised her Love Canal neighbours in Niagara Falls after discovering their homes and school sat on a buried chemical dump. Their campaign led to the evacuation of hundreds of families and helped bring about the federal Superfund law in 1980.
Brockovich helped build the case against PG&E for contaminating Hinkley's groundwater with chromium-6. The 1996 settlement of 333 million US dollars was then the largest of its kind.

Lovins co-founded the Rocky Mountain Institute in 1982 and championed 'soft energy paths' built on efficiency and renewables decades before they became mainstream. His work on whole-system design has helped companies and governments cut energy waste.
Krenak's 1987 speech to Brazil's constituent assembly helped secure Indigenous rights in the constitution. He became the first Indigenous member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters.

Hill lived for 738 days, from 1997 to 1999, in a 1,500-year-old coast redwood called Luna to stop it being logged. Her protest ended in an agreement protecting the tree and a buffer zone around it, and she has since campaigned for forests and social change.

Chouinard built Patagonia into a company that gives one percent of sales to environmental groups and campaigns for public lands. In 2022 he gave away the company, transferring it to a trust and a nonprofit so that its profits fund the fight against climate change.

With her late husband Douglas, Tompkins bought and restored vast areas of Patagonia and then gave them away, including a roughly one-million-acre donation to Chile in 2018 that helped create five new national parks. Her foundation also rewilds lost species such as jaguars in Argentina's Iberá wetlands.

Tompkins, co-founder of The North Face and Esprit, used his fortune to buy and protect more than two million acres of wild land in Chile and Argentina. The land he and Kristine Tompkins conserved became the foundation of several national parks, including Pumalín.
